blocks.text: Acoma Pueblo History and Culture
Origins colonial encounters and a living nation

Acoma Pueblo is a federally recognized Native nation in west central New Mexico. Its historic mesa village, Haak’u, is often called Sky City. Acoma’s history includes centuries of farming, Spanish conquest, a major revolt and long struggles over land and water. Its people have maintained their community through these changes and continue to shape its future through tribal government, art and language preservation. [1, 3, 16]
The people and their homeland

Acoma lies about 60 miles west of Albuquerque. The nation includes the mesa village and communities below it, including Acomita and McCartys. The Rio San Jose connects these communities to a wider farming landscape. The word Pueblo comes from Spanish and means town or village. Spaniards used it for many settled Native communities, but those communities had their own languages, governments and identities. Acoma is one distinct nation within this larger Pueblo world. [2, 3]

Acoma people speak a form of Keres, also called Keresan. Other Keres speaking Pueblos include Laguna, Zia and several communities along the Rio Grande. Shared language does not make them one political community. Their separate histories and local traditions matter when studying them. Acoma’s own account explains its name as a place always prepared and identifies Haak’u as a homeland with deep spiritual meaning. [1, 2]
How old is Acoma

Acoma is among the oldest continuously occupied communities in what is now the United States. A precise founding year is harder to establish. The Pueblo’s website states that continuous occupation is accepted from at least about 1200 CE. The National Park Service places the oldest surviving remains around 1100 CE. These dates describe surviving material evidence. They do not establish the beginning of Acoma identity or the earliest human presence in the surrounding country. [1, 4]

Acoma oral history places the community’s relationship with its homeland in a much deeper past. Oral traditions carry knowledge about belonging, sacred places and obligations between generations. Archaeology studies physical remains such as buildings and pottery. Each supplies evidence about the past, although they answer different questions. Describing Acoma as an ancient living community is better supported than assigning it a single certain birthday. [1, 4]
Farming family and village life

Agriculture helped support settled Pueblo life. Corn, beans and squash were major foods across the region. Farmers worked within a dry environment where the timing and movement of water shaped the growing season. Food production was tied to cooperation between families and to ceremonies concerning rain and the land. Trade connected farming communities with neighboring peoples and helped circulate food, pottery and other goods. [2]

Family ties also shaped Acoma society. Acoma has a matrilineal tradition, meaning that family descent is traced through the mother’s line. Women’s relationships to homes and property could carry legal force. In a later account published by the University of California Davis School of Law, attorney Michael Taylor recalled an Acoma marriage case in which his co-counsel Ruth Paisano explained the wife’s property rights under Pueblo law. The example shows why outside assumptions about marriage and ownership can misread Acoma institutions. It is a recollection of one case rather than a complete statement of present tribal law. [17]

The mesa made the village easier to defend, but daily life also depended on the valleys below. Early Spanish visitors described houses several stories high and abundant food stores. Building and maintaining the settlement required generations of skilled work. [5]
Spanish arrival and the attack of 1599

Hernando de Alvarado visited Acoma during the Coronado expedition in 1540. Further expeditions followed in the 1580s. In 1598, Juan de Oñate brought colonists into New Mexico. Acoma’s tribal history describes confusion over an act of obedience to the Spanish king and the conflict that followed. [5]

In December 1598, a confrontation involving demands for provisions ended with the deaths of Captain Juan de Zaldívar and other Spanish soldiers at Acoma. Oñate ordered a punitive expedition under Juan’s brother, Vicente de Zaldívar. In January 1599, Spanish forces attacked the mesa community, used a cannon and burned buildings. Acoma surrendered after several days of fighting. [6]

Hundreds of Acoma people died. About 800 is a frequently repeated estimate, but the surviving accounts do not support an exact modern count. Historian Henry Warner Bowden’s published references give a range of 600 to 800 deaths and roughly 500 people enslaved. The Pueblo’s own history reports about 500 prisoners. These figures establish the scale of the disaster while leaving uncertainty about the totals. [5, 18]

The sentence recorded in Neil Mangum’s National Park Service history ordered men over 25 to lose a foot and provide 20 years of forced service. Younger males and women in specified age groups also faced long terms of forced service. Describing these punishments as sentences makes clear what the Spanish authorities ordered; it does not prove how every punishment was carried out. Calling the service slavery or enslavement conveys the coercion more clearly than the colonial phrase personal service. [6]

Spanish authorities later investigated Oñate. Acoma’s history records convictions for unjustified executions and indiscriminate killing, followed by banishment from New Mexico. Spanish officials themselves judged his conduct unlawful, although the investigation could not undo the damage. [5]
Rebuilding and San Esteban del Rey

Acoma people rebuilt after the destruction. Colonial rule continued, and civil officials and Franciscan missionaries competed over authority. The Pueblo’s account describes Native complaints about abuses and orders issued in 1620 concerning Pueblo administration. It also places Fray Juan Ramirez’s arrival at Acoma in 1629 within renewed Franciscan efforts to establish missions. [7]

The surviving San Esteban del Rey Mission Church is usually associated with building work that began after Ramirez arrived. The National Park Service cautions that its exact construction dates are uncertain. Acoma workers carried materials up the mesa, including large roof beams brought from distant mountains. The church’s size reflects both the demands of the mission system and the skill and labor of the people who built it. [4]

The church remains part of Acoma heritage. The Pueblo identifies its caretakers as the Gaugashti, men with a continuing responsibility to maintain the building. Its survival depends on work by successive generations. Their care of the structure gives the history an Acoma perspective: a building introduced through colonial rule can acquire lasting local responsibilities and meanings. [8]
The Pueblo Revolt and renewed Spanish rule

In 1680, Acoma joined other Pueblo communities in a revolt against Spanish rule. The uprising challenged colonial power and the suppression of Native religious life. At Acoma, the resident priest and other Spaniards were killed, while the mission church survived. Spanish control returned to Acoma by 1699. Catholic observance and Indigenous religious practices continued together in the community. [4]

The sources require care. Bowden points out that much surviving written evidence comes from Europeans whose accounts carried their own religious and political assumptions. He also notes the loss of church and government records during the fighting of 1680 to 1696. His article was published in 1975 and uses some language now considered dated. Its discussion of the uneven written record remains useful, especially when read alongside Acoma’s own histories. [18]
Mexico the United States and land rights

Mexican independence in 1821 placed New Mexico under a new national government. United States forces occupied the region in 1846, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred it to the United States in 1848. Acoma people continued living on their homeland through each change of outside government. [3]

Acoma and Laguna also had disputes of their own. Deborah A. Rosen’s legal history article describes a conflict over a painting of Saint Joseph shortly after the U.S. occupation. Acoma claimed it had lent the painting to Laguna for Holy Week and that Laguna had refused to return it. Both communities claimed ownership and associated it with life giving rain. The example connects religion, agriculture and property within the changing legal world of nineteenth century New Mexico. This account follows the article’s publicly available extract. [9]

Acoma’s official landholding record shows that its territory was shaped by several legal processes. The document lists an older Pueblo grant, federal actions, land exchanges and purchases. Examples include a railroad exchange in 1939, a federal act in 1949 and the purchase of Red Lake Ranch in 1989. These entries show sustained efforts to strengthen the land base. The document includes transactions through 2008 and should be read as a dated record, rather than a current acreage total. [11]

Government also carries older symbols of authority. Acoma’s Canes of Power account describes silver headed staffs passed between Pueblo governors. Such objects became part of the public recognition of Pueblo leadership under Spanish rule. Their continuing importance helps explain how Acoma institutions could adapt forms associated with outside governments while maintaining community authority. [10]
Water and the farming landscape

Access to land did not guarantee access to water. In congressional testimony in 2022, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs Bryan Newland described the effects of upstream development on Acoma and Laguna. Diversions associated with Fort Wingate and later settlements reduced water reaching the Rio San Jose. A dam on Bluewater Creek and increased groundwater pumping caused further losses. [12]

The testimony also linked twentieth century uranium mining and milling to declining groundwater and spring flows. These changes harmed the water supply on which Pueblo agriculture depended. The history matters because water disputes concern the ability to keep farming and sustain community life. The 2022 testimony explains the background to settlement proposals at that time; it does not establish the current status of those proposals. [12]
Pottery and artistic knowledge

Acoma pottery is known for thin walls, light surfaces and carefully painted designs. Geometric patterns, birds and plant forms appear in its artistic traditions. Wichita State University’s Holmes Museum identifies Lucy Lewis and Marie Chino as important artists who adapted older designs to the vessels they made. Pottery connected household knowledge with changing opportunities to earn income through sales. [3]

Lucy M. Lewis learned by watching other women and by working with clay herself. The Smithsonian describes her fine black line designs and her use of ancestral pottery as a source of ideas. She sold work along roads such as Route 66 before her pottery entered major museum collections. Her example shows how individual creativity could grow from community learning. Children and grandchildren continued making pottery, passing skills through family relationships. [13]
Language preservation and cultural ownership

Acoma’s cultural preservation history describes a community survey in 1997 that found fewer children learning Keres as their first language. In 1999, the Pueblo established a language retention program and a historic preservation office. The preservation work included building skills, pottery, weaving and other knowledge. These efforts treated language and culture as responsibilities to younger generations. [14]

The Pueblo’s language program describes a dictionary project begun in 2017, with fluent speakers reviewing words and phrases. Its public account explains that culturally sensitive terms are excluded. Writing teaching materials represents an adaptation for a language traditionally passed through speech. It also demonstrates that the community can decide what knowledge belongs in public resources and what remains restricted. [15]

The recovery of a ceremonial shield provides another example of cultural ownership. A shield sacred to Acoma appeared in a Paris auction catalog in 2016. Tribal identification and a U.S. legal action helped secure its release in 2019. The Justice Department explained that, under Acoma law, an individual could not transfer it outside the Pueblo. Its caretaker held a responsibility to the community. The case shows why possession by a collector does not necessarily establish a right to sell a sacred object. [16]

Acoma’s continuing history is visible in these specific activities: families teach pottery, caretakers maintain the church and language workers develop materials for learners. Land purchases and water claims address the resources needed to sustain the community. Studying these efforts alongside conquest and resistance gives a fuller account of how Acoma people have maintained their nation. [8, 11–16]

blocks.text: Achumawi History and Culture
The people of the Pit River region of northeastern California

The Achumawi are Indigenous people whose communities developed along the Pit River and its tributaries in northeastern California. Their history connects local government, skilled fishing practices and spiritual ties to place with survival through violent displacement. Achumawi people remain part of the wider Pit River Tribe and continue work to protect land and teach language. [1, 4, 5, 10, 14]
Names and identity

Achumawi, also spelled Achomawi, is commonly used for nine related Indigenous bands of northeastern California. Ajumawi and Ahjumawi are other spellings associated especially with the Fall River band. The name is often translated as “river people.” California State Parks also gives the translation “where the waters come together.” These different spellings reflect different ways of writing Indigenous speech in English. [2, 3, 5]

The wider Pit River Tribe includes eleven autonomous bands. Nine traditionally spoke varieties of Achumawi. The Atsugewi and Aporige bands spoke varieties of Atsugewi. Achumawi and Atsugewi are related languages, but they have distinct histories. Using “Achumawi” for all eleven bands can hide that difference. [1, 2, 4]

Using the spellings on the tribe’s official website, the nine Achumawi bands are Ajumawi, Astarawi, Atwamsini, Hammawi, Hewisedawi, Ilmawi, Itsatawi, Kosalektawi and Madesi. Older accounts often use different names or divide local groups differently. C. Hart Merriam’s 1926 study shows how widely names varied between neighboring communities. [1, 2]
Homeland and the river

The traditional Achumawi language area follows the Pit River from the edge of the northern Sacramento Valley toward Goose Lake. The wider Pit River Tribe describes its ancestral homeland as the “100-mile square,” covering parts of Shasta, Siskiyou, Modoc and Lassen counties. This describes a broad homeland. It should not be confused with the boundaries of a single present-day reservation. [1, 4, 10]

The region includes river valleys, marshes, forests and volcanic uplands. In the Fall River basin, underground water emerges through springs around lava flows. Big Lake, the Tule River and several streams meet in the area now protected as Ahjumawi Lava Springs State Park. Such places supplied dependable water and supported fish and other foods. [5, 12]

This geography helps explain why local communities developed around particular stretches of water. A shared language connected the bands, while different valleys and fishing places supported local identities. Their history therefore needs to be understood at both levels: the larger Achumawi population and the individual communities within it. [2, 3]
Food homes and daily work

Fishing and gathering were central to daily life. Foods included fish, roots, seeds, berries and acorns, with local supplies varying across the homeland. Winter houses were partly underground and had sloping bark roofs. Lighter shelters of brush or tule mats served during warmer weather. Larger communal structures provided places for gatherings. These choices suited the seasons and materials available nearby. [3]

Deer provided meat and hides for clothing and equipment. Hunters dug pits along animal trails to catch them. Settlers used this practice to name the Pit River and then applied the river’s name to its Indigenous peoples. Historical descriptions also mention deerskin quivers, moccasins and other garments. The name “Pit River” preserves an outsider’s description of one hunting method. [6]
Stone fish traps and knowledge of water

The stone fish traps at Ahjumawi are a clear example of local engineering. People arranged rocks near the shore so that fresh spring water attracted trout and Sacramento suckers. The structures guided fish into shallow areas where they could be caught during winter spawning. Their builders needed to understand water flow, fish behavior and the shape of the shoreline. [5]

California State Parks describes a practice of stopping the harvest after a self-imposed limit. The traps then provided protected places for fish to spawn. Food gathering included decisions about future fish supplies. The surviving structures are evidence of a managed fishing landscape and the work required to maintain it. [5]
Family ceremonies and spiritual life

Historical accounts describe ceremonies marking a young person’s passage into adulthood, exchanges of gifts between families at marriage and public mourning after death. Healers could be women or men. These accounts show the importance of family relationships and ceremonial responsibilities, although practices could differ between communities and change over time. [6]

Jaime de Angulo’s account of Achumawi spiritual thought records people speaking of life and power in trees, rocks, water and mountains. In one conversation, a man described greeting the beings around him and seeking friendly relationships with them. In this account, people lived among other beings with whom they had obligations. A place could matter as a source of food and as part of a spiritual relationship. [7]

De Angulo’s essay was first published in French in 1928. Annette Boushey’s English translation appeared in 1975. It preserves valuable testimony, but the interviews, translation and author’s explanations all shaped the published account. His broad statements about an entire people should be read with care. [7]

Another important work is Annikadel, attributed to Istet Woiche and recorded and edited by C. Hart Merriam. Shasta Public Libraries lists the University of Arizona Press edition of 1992 and its earlier publication history. It is a useful starting point for studying Achumawi oral literature, with attention to the difference between the storyteller’s words and the editor’s presentation. [15]
Trade and relations with neighboring peoples

Pit River communities participated in a wider network of trade across northern California and southern Oregon. Thomas N. Layton’s study of early nineteenth-century commerce discusses Pit River bows and beads moving through regional trading systems. The Sáttítla highlands also supplied obsidian, a volcanic glass used for cutting tools and valued blades. Obsidian from this region circulated through broad Indigenous trade networks. [8, 13]

Some relationships also involved warfare and enslavement. Layton discusses historical reports of Klamath and Modoc raiders taking Pit River captives, especially women and children, for sale through networks reaching The Dalles on the Columbia River. He also notes evidence that some eastern Pit River communities had friendly relations with Modoc neighbors. [8]

These differences matter. A record of raids does not describe every relationship between whole peoples. Trade, kinship and conflict could exist in the same region. Layton also identifies limits in the surviving evidence and distinguishes documented accounts from his own arguments about changes in settlement. [8]
Settlement violence and forced removal

Growing settler occupation in the 1850s brought conflict over the homeland. A state cultural resources study describes killings following the destruction of Lockhart Ferry in 1856, the establishment of Fort Crook in 1857 and forced removal to Round Valley in 1859. It also records disease and later returns by Achumawi and Atsugewi people. [3]

The California Indian History archive indexes contemporary records that describe killings of Pit River women and children. Its entry for the Nevada Democrat of October 5, 1859 records a report blaming white attackers for a massacre that an earlier account had blamed on Indigenous people. Other entries describe the burning of villages and the taking of prisoners. [9]

These reports require careful reading. Newspapers and military officials sometimes repeated rumors, defended their conduct or used hostile language. Their accounts should not automatically be accepted as complete or impartial. Even so, the records show that violence reached families and settlements. Describing the period only as fighting between soldiers and warriors would leave out central parts of what happened. [9]

The effects of removal extended beyond physical distance. For communities whose homes and food supplies centered on particular rivers, removal broke access to those places. Returning home helped people maintain local ties, but it did not restore the earlier balance of power over land and resources. [3, 5, 10]
Government and the struggle to protect land

The Pit River Tribe continues as a federally recognized tribal government made up of eleven bands. Its constitution states that a formal written constitution was adopted on August 16, 1964. The version held by the National Indian Law Library, updated in July 2005, describes elected band representatives serving on the Tribal Council. [5, 10]

The constitution’s stated purposes include protecting ancestral lands and resources, maintaining order, promoting the welfare of descendants and preserving culture and identity. It presents sovereignty as an inherent right of the people. The written constitution gave a formal structure to shared government while recognizing the component bands. [10]

Protecting the Medicine Lake Highlands became an important part of this work. In Pit River Tribe v. Bureau of Land Management, decided on September 19, 2019, the Ninth Circuit upheld a ruling favorable to the tribe and allied organizations in a dispute over geothermal leases. The court held that unproven leases could not receive the challenged forty-year continuation merely because one lease in the unit had been proven. [11]

The decision concerned how federal leasing law applied. It did not settle every issue of tribal ownership or religious freedom. Its historical importance lies in the tribe’s continued use of the courts to challenge decisions affecting its homeland. [11]
Sáttítla and living cultural ties

Medicine Lake and the surrounding highlands remain important to Pit River people and several neighboring Indigenous peoples. The Forest Service describes the area as central to Pit River creation stories and cultural health. Volcanic rock stores water underground and feeds spring systems beyond the highlands. Religious concerns and the protection of water therefore meet in the same place. [12]

On January 14, 2025, President Joe Biden signed the proclamation establishing Sáttítla Highlands National Monument. The monument covers 224,676 acres. The proclamation recognizes the area’s Indigenous cultural importance, obsidian resources and water systems. It also directs federal managers to seek tribal expertise and provide for continued traditional uses under applicable law. [12, 13]

The designation followed years of tribal advocacy and litigation. It protected federal land through monument status while leaving the Forest Service responsible for management. It did not return the whole Achumawi or Pit River ancestral homeland to tribal ownership. [11, 13]
Language and cultural continuity

Achumawi and Atsugewi are generally grouped as the Palaihnihan language family. Their proposed connection to a larger Hokan family remains a hypothesis. Berkeley’s California Language Archive points readers to dictionaries, teaching materials and linguistic studies. Its speaker estimate draws on work published in 2011, so it should not be treated as a new count for 2026. [4]

The Pit River Tribe posted an announcement for language sessions on March 2, 2026. This is direct evidence of present-day work to teach and maintain language. It also shows why an account of the Achumawi needs to include the people living now, alongside older descriptions preserved by anthropologists. [14]

Shasta Public Libraries’ California Indian Library Collections bibliography provides routes into language recordings, photographs, oral literature and scholarly studies. Many older works remain useful, but their terminology and conclusions need to be weighed against tribal accounts and later research. Cultural continuity includes the authority of Achumawi people to interpret these materials and decide how knowledge is passed on. [15]

blocks.text: The Huetar People of Costa Rica
Culture History and Timeline

The Huetar are an Indigenous people of central Costa Rica in Central America. Their ancestors lived across much of the Central Valley and neighboring regions when Spanish forces expanded into the interior during the sixteenth century. Huetar communities continue today, especially in Quitirrisí and Zapatón. Their history includes resistance to conquest and efforts to pass cultural knowledge to younger generations. [5, 7, 13]

The loss of the Huetar language did not end the Huetar people. Research in Quitirrisí documents a strong sense of community identity grounded in ancestry, place and inherited traditions. This distinction matters when reading older accounts that describe Indigenous culture mainly in terms of what disappeared. [12]
Homeland and communities

The historic Huetar homeland included the Central Valley and areas around the Virilla and Grande de Tárcoles rivers, extending toward the Pacific coast. Linguistic and historical evidence also links Huetar speech with areas farther east. These were regions of contact and movement, so the edges of a cultural area should not be treated as fixed national borders. [1, 5]

The two recognized Huetar Indigenous territories are Quitirrisí in the canton of Mora and Zapatón in the canton of Puriscal. Both are in San José Province. A canton is a local administrative division. Huetar families also live outside these territories. [10, 11]

Costa Rica’s 2011 census recorded 3,461 people who identified as Huetar nationwide. Of these, 1,354 lived in the two Huetar territories, about 39 percent of the total. These are dated census figures, not a population estimate for 2026. They show why the people cannot be counted only by looking at the two territories. [9]
Society before Spanish rule

Huetar communities formed chiefdoms, often called cacicazgos in Spanish. A cacique was a political leader. Larger leaders exercised authority over smaller communities, but the strength of these ties could change. Chiefs helped organize production, exchange and collective activity. Differences in rank shaped political and economic life. [4]

Garabito ruled an important western domain. Guarco and his successor Correque were associated with a major eastern center. Pacaca was another significant chiefdom. The common division into eastern and western Huetar “kingdoms” is a broad outline. Other centers also had separate political relationships. The Huetar did not form one unified state. [2, 5]

Archaeology provides evidence of skilled work in stone and clay. Decorated metates, or grinding stones, and pottery appear in the older societies of central Costa Rica. Some objects served purposes connected with rank or burial as well as practical work. Archaeological evidence and colonial records describe different parts of this long history and should be read together. [4]
Food farming and skilled work

Inherited farming practices included planting maize, beans and squash together. These crops helped one another: bean plants added nitrogen to the soil, while broad squash leaves shaded the ground. Farming required knowledge of local plants, soils and seasons. [3]

The University of Costa Rica’s School of Nutrition describes living Huetar traditions within a wider regional food culture. Foods used in this region include maize, beans, squash, cassava and leafy plants. Knowledge of local ingredients and food preparation remains part of cultural life. Many foods are shared with neighboring communities, and contemporary cooking reflects both Indigenous inheritance and later changes. [8]

Basketry is one of the clearest continuing Huetar crafts. Artisans work with plant fibers to make baskets, hats and other useful objects. Documented traditions also include natural dyes, clay vessels, gourd containers and cordage. Preparing the material is part of the skill: fibers must be selected and processed before they can be woven. Selling crafts also provides income for some families. [6, 7, 8]
The Huetar language

Huetar once served as a lingua franca, a language used between people from different communities. Its wide use reflected the political importance and connections of Huetar societies. University linguistic research places its disappearance as an everyday spoken language around the end of the eighteenth century, although fragments may have remained later. An exact date for the last speaker is not established. [1]

Researchers preserve evidence from names, colonial records and words that survived in Costa Rican Spanish. The language is usually discussed in relation to the Chibchan family, but its precise classification remains uncertain because the surviving evidence is limited. Scholars cannot recover a complete language simply from a list of place names and isolated words. [1, 5]

Linguist Adolfo Constenla Umaña also stressed a major problem: colonial grammars and religious texts reported to have existed had not been located. His 1984 study shows why claims about Huetar grammar and word origins need careful checking. A surviving name may identify a person or place without preserving its original meaning. [5]
Spanish conquest and colonial change

In 1561 Juan de Cavallón’s expedition entered the Central Valley. Juan Vázquez de Coronado followed as a leading Spanish official in 1562. Garabito resisted Spanish demands and remained a major obstacle to Spanish control. [2]

The conquest brought violence, epidemic disease and demands for Indigenous labor. It also weakened communities’ control over food production and land. Displacement broke connections among families and settlements. These pressures help explain the long process through which Spanish became dominant and many older institutions changed. [7]

In 1569 Governor Perafán de Ribera distributed Indigenous tributaries through the encomienda system. Holders received claims to tribute from assigned Indigenous communities. Colonists also extracted personal labor even when such demands violated legal restrictions. [2]

Colonial accounts preserve valuable evidence, but their authors’ aims shaped their descriptions. Historians compare these records with archaeology and later community testimony. The surviving documents also leave gaps, particularly concerning the Huetar language. [5]
Land and migration in the twentieth century

Historian Orlando Amaris Cervantes studied Huetar migration between 1900 and 1955 through historical evidence and oral accounts. Some families moved from Mora toward southern Puriscal, including Zapatón and Mastatal. [3]

He distinguishes the wider spread of coffee in the Central Valley from the stronger local expansion of cattle pasture in Mora. Pasture reduced land available for food crops and for resting exhausted soils. Repeated cultivation on the remaining land made farming harder. Families sought better land elsewhere because their ability to support themselves was under pressure. [3]
Beliefs memory and identity

Community accounts recorded for Costa Rica’s Ministry of Public Education describe respect for forests, rivers and places associated with spiritual stories. They also describe Catholic worship and funeral practices. Inherited ideas and Christianity could exist within the same community, although beliefs varied among individuals. [7]
Elders’ stories preserve community memory. Their meanings can change as families pass them down, so a modern telling does not establish the exact form of a ceremony before Spanish contact. [7]

A 2008 study by Marjorie Moreno Salas surveyed 90 people in Quitirrisí and found a high level of ethnic identity. Ancestral traditions and residence in the community helped sustain belonging. This was a study of one community and sample, not a survey of every Huetar person. It nevertheless gives direct evidence that Huetar identity continued despite language loss. [12]

Anthropologist Raquel Ornat Clemente studied changes in Quitirrisí’s identity over time. Her work describes people adapting their cultural life under changing social and political conditions. Cultural change alone does not establish whether a community remains Indigenous. [4]
Territorial rights and continuing cultural work

Quitirrisí received legal recognition in 1976. Later measures defined and revised its boundaries. A 2001 decree acknowledged that earlier delimitation had not adequately reflected the community’s cultural and economic life. This is evidence that recognizing a territory and defining an adequate territory are separate tasks. [10]

Zapatón was declared an Indigenous settlement in 1981 and an Indigenous reserve in 1982. A 1988 opinion from Costa Rica’s Attorney General’s Office affirmed that it had reserve status and fell under the Indigenous Law. These measures recognized an existing people and community. [11]

Legal recognition did not settle control of land. Research published in 2016 documented unequal access to land within Huetar territories and pressure to seek employment elsewhere. It linked these problems with the difficulty of maintaining farming and other activities. The figures in that research describe earlier conditions and should not be read as a new land survey. [9]

Cultural work continues through teaching and community projects. The University of Costa Rica’s Quizarco project, listed for 2023 to 2026, addressed how schools in Quitirrisí and Zapatón could teach Huetar culture through local experience. Its description records a concern from community leaders that a general national curriculum needed to reflect each territory’s life. [13]

In 2024 the University for Peace announced a book project presenting Quitirrisí elders’ knowledge in their own words. The project began after elders asked to preserve their stories in 2022. Its announced title was Conocimientos de la Cultura Huetar de Quitirrisí. This work places community members in the role of authors and teachers of their own history. [14]
Timeline
The early dates concern the societies and events described in surviving records. They do not mark a single founding date for the Huetar people.

blocks.text: Chinook Culture History and Timeline
The lower Columbia River peoples and the Chinook Indian Nation
Research checked 18 October 2026

The Chinook are a living Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest. Their history centers on the lower Columbia River, its estuary and the nearby Pacific coast. Fishing, canoe travel, cedar woodworking and trade connected their villages. This study explains that culture, follows the effects of foreign trade and American settlement and traces the continuing work of the Chinook Indian Nation. [1,2]

Two related subjects appear throughout the study. Chinookan peoples are the broader group of communities linked by related languages along the Columbia. The present Chinook Indian Nation represents five westernmost Chinookan communities near the river’s mouth. Keeping that difference clear prevents the history of one nation from being confused with the history of every Chinookan people. [1]
Homeland and identity

The Nation identifies its core territory along the lower river from near Oak Point, west of present Longview, to the Pacific, together with neighboring coastal lands. Its five constituent peoples are listed below. The Oregon–Washington border is a later political boundary across a much older network of relationships. [1]

Ancestral area in present day terms
Lower Chinook

Clatsop

blocks.text: Farther upriver, other Chinookan communities lived through the Portland Basin and Columbia Gorge toward The Dalles. Scholars reconstruct a landscape of many named villages rather than one centrally governed nation. A modern village study identifies more than eighty villages and larger groupings between Astoria and Cascade Locks, with an estimated population of at least 15,000 in the early nineteenth century. Those figures describe the wider region, not the five communities alone. [2]
Culture and daily life
Fishing and seasonal food

Salmon runs helped organize the year. Chinook fishers also caught sturgeon, steelhead, eulachon and herring. They used nets, hooks, harpoons and other tools suited to particular waters and fish. Fish could be eaten fresh or smoke dried for later meals and exchange. Clams from Willapa Bay and other coastal foods broadened the diet. [4]

Roots, berries, wild game and birds also supplied food. Wapato, an edible wetland tuber, moved through river trade. Families used established villages together with seasonal locations that gave access to changing supplies. Food storage made it possible to live in substantial settlements through the wet winter. The economy depended on detailed knowledge of local waters, plants and animal behavior. [15,23]
Cedar houses and household life

The best known Chinookan homes were plankhouses built with cedar posts, beams and split boards. Several related families could share a large house. Hearths provided heat and cooking space, while raised platforms along the walls served for sleeping and storage. A house also supported food processing, craft work and ceremonies. [3]

House sizes and arrangements varied. Some households moved boards between seasonal house frames, which sometimes led visiting outsiders to mistake a temporarily unused settlement for an abandoned one. Archaeological examples from the lower Columbia show that recognizable plankhouse traditions extend back roughly 2,000 years or more. This evidence supports long cultural continuity without assigning a precise founding date to the modern Nation. [3]
Canoes and river knowledge

Cedar canoes carried people, food and trade goods through rivers, bays and coastal waters. Builders shaped vessels for different conditions and decorated some with carved or painted animal designs. Large examples could carry twenty to thirty people and cargo. Successful travel required knowledge of tides, currents, weather and the dangerous Columbia River mouth. [5]

In 1806, Meriwether Lewis admired how safely local people handled waves that frightened him. His account is evidence of Chinookan skill, although it remains an outsider’s description. Canoes were valuable products of trained labor and inherited knowledge. They also remain part of Chinook community life through the Canoe Family and cultural gatherings. [5,21]
Clothing weaving and art

Clothing suited the damp climate. Cedar bark, beargrass and animal skins were used for garments and headwear. Visitors admired water resistant hats and sea otter robes. Some Chinook people also wore clothing acquired from foreign sailors, showing how readily new goods could enter existing ways of life. [6]

Women’s basketry and textiles served household needs and produced income. Women owned property and could retain earnings from their work. Basket sales continued into markets involving settlers, tourists and collectors. Many museums preserved the objects while failing to record their makers’ names, leaving a serious gap in the historical record. [8]

Contemporary Chinookan artists continue and renew local carving traditions. The Nation documents work by Tony A. Johnson, including carved kingfishers and a house post design. Such work places Chinookan visual culture in present public spaces as well as in museums and historic collections. [24]
Families leadership and social rank

The village and extended household were central to political life. Leaders drew authority from inherited rights, family connections, ability and the respect of others. Important decisions could involve more than one leader. Early foreign visitors often used the word chief too broadly, making local authority appear more centralized than it was. [2,7]

Women could hold leadership positions, and rights could pass through either parent. At the same time, historical Chinook society had clear inequalities. High status families, commoners and enslaved people occupied different positions. A careful account must include both women’s authority and the existence of slavery. Neither a uniformly equal society nor a single all powerful chief describes the evidence well. [7,8]
Language and communication

The original Chinookan languages and Chinuk Wawa are different. Chinuk Wawa, often called Chinook Jargon in older writing, became a shared language used among people who did not have the same first language. Its vocabulary drew on Chinookan and other Indigenous languages as well as French and English. It spread widely through the fur trade. [9]

Scholars disagree about exactly when and how Chinuk Wawa formed. It should not simply be called a language invented by white traders. Linguist Henry Zenk emphasizes the major role Chinookan speakers played in its formation. Today, language teaching and renewal continue in several Native communities, notably Grand Ronde. Those efforts belong to distinct communities within a shared regional language history. [9]
Ceremony and relationships with the living world

The First Salmon Ceremony publicly expresses the importance of salmon beyond food or trade. The Chinook Indian Nation describes honoring the first fish, preparing it over an alder fire and returning its bones to the Columbia. Children take part and learn from experienced cooks and community leaders. The ceremony connects respect for salmon with hopes for their continued return. [10]

Historical accounts also describe guardian spirit songs, dancing, feasts and the giving of gifts. Anthropologist Verne Ray warned that the word potlatch can hide differences between Lower Chinook practices and ceremonies farther north. It is safer to describe the particular gathering than to assume that all Northwest Coast peoples followed one identical system. [11]

Charles Cultee, a Chinook knowledge keeper at Bay Center, supplied Franz Boas with extensive language and cultural material in the early 1890s. Their work produced Chinook Texts and Kathlamet Texts. These records preserve important knowledge, but they also passed through an outside collector’s questions, transcription and translation. Cultee’s contribution deserves attention alongside Boas’s published name. [12]
History and major turning points
A river economy before foreign settlement

Chinookan communities had established villages, fisheries and exchange networks long before foreign ships entered the Columbia. People near the river mouth occupied a useful position between inland communities and coastal traffic. Trade helped connect local households to goods and relationships well beyond their own villages. Geography mattered because the river linked otherwise distant places. [2,23]
Maritime trade and powerful negotiators

Robert Gray entered the Columbia in 1792, helping open a period of expanding maritime fur trading. Foreign merchants entered an existing Native trading world. Chinook leaders negotiated prices, directed access to goods and built alliances with newcomers. The arrival of imported objects did not immediately erase local control over exchange. [13,22]

Concomly, also often spelled Comcomly, became the best known Lower Chinook headman of this era. Born around 1765, he increased his influence through trade and family alliances. After Fort Astoria was established in 1811, he worked to channel exchanges through his own network. His position changed as the Hudson’s Bay Company shifted its center to Fort Vancouver in 1825. He died during the malaria epidemic in 1830. His influence should not be confused with rule over every Chinookan community. [13]
Lewis and Clark in Chinook country

The expedition spent the winter of 1805–1806 at Fort Clatsop in Clatsop territory. Coboway, a Clatsop village leader, gave permission for the winter house and maintained contact with the visitors. Local people traded food, clothing and other supplies with the expedition. The relationship involved repeated negotiation and practical help. [15]

It also included a serious breach of trust. On 18 March 1806, John Ordway recorded that expedition members took a Clatsop canoe and concealed it while the local chief was visiting. The university edition identifies this as theft. This incident is a useful reminder that the journals record the visitors’ actions and priorities, rather than a neutral account of an equal friendship. [16]
Epidemics and loss

Introduced infections caused catastrophic losses. Robert Boyd dates the earliest documented Oregon smallpox epidemic most likely to about 1781, while noting uncertainty. Malaria outbreaks began in 1830 and were especially destructive through 1834. A further smallpox epidemic struck lower Columbia communities in 1853. [14]

These deaths removed relatives, leaders and specialists who carried essential knowledge. Survivors combined households and sometimes left villages. Losses also weakened communities as settler pressure increased. Precise totals remain uncertain, and very high estimates for the Portland Basin should not be treated as an exact count for every community at the river mouth. [14]
Treaties settlement and refusal to leave

In August 1851, Anson Dart negotiated the Tansy Point treaties with Chinook and neighboring peoples. Chinook leaders pressed to remain near their homes and ancestors. The agreements included provisions for staying within their homelands, but the Senate did not ratify them. Settler occupation continued without fulfillment of the promises made at the negotiations. [17,25]

At the Chehalis River negotiations in 1855, Governor Isaac Stevens sought relocation away from Chinook homelands. Chinook representatives refused to agree. James Swan’s account records the importance of family burial places and the danger leaders associated with being moved among other peoples. This was a specific refusal of removal, not a refusal of all negotiation with the United States. [26]
Community survival through the twentieth century

Some Chinook descendants lived on reservations or became citizens of other tribal nations. Others maintained connections in the lower Columbia and Willapa Bay communities. The Chinook Indian Nation and the larger population of people with Chinookan ancestry therefore overlap without being identical. [19]

Chinook children attended federal Indian boarding schools, including Chemawa and Cushman. Community members also pursued land claims, maintained enrollment records and developed written forms of government. These efforts show families adapting their organization while working to protect relationships, land interests and cultural knowledge. [22]

Modern scholars and tribal researchers use archaeology, family testimony, government rolls and written records together. Each supplies a different part of the picture. A village site can show how a household worked, while oral history can explain connections to place that a census or traveler’s journal may miss. [2,17,22]
Federal recognition and the Nation today

In January 2001, Assistant Secretary Kevin Gover signed a favorable final determination acknowledging the Chinook Indian Tribe or Chinook Nation. The decision relied on historical records, interviews and an interpretation of earlier congressional actions. It followed a recognition effort for which the Nation had notified the Bureau of Indian Affairs of its intent to petition in 1979. [18]

In 2002, the Interior Department reversed that determination after reconsideration. The department disputed how the earlier decision had interpreted evidence of community, political authority and prior government acknowledgment. The Chinook contest that outcome. The disagreement concerns the federal acknowledgment requirements and how historical evidence is evaluated. [19]

As of this study, the Chinook Indian Nation is not on the federal list of recognized tribes. The January 2026 list confirms that federal position. This legal status does not mean Chinook people disappeared. Their government, gatherings, family networks and cultural programs continue. Recognition matters because it establishes a formal federal relationship tied to services, funding and protections. [20,21]

The Nation’s Culture Committee organizes the First Salmon Ceremony, Winter Gathering, Story Gathering and Tansy Point Treaty Days. Drummers, singers, dancers and the Canoe Family help carry these practices forward. Art and language work make cultural renewal part of present community life. [21,24]

Reconnection with land also continues. Chinook scholar Rachel Lynne Cushman dates the closing of the Nation’s purchase of ten acres of treaty grounds at Tansy Point to 8 April 2019. In her 2026 account, she describes habitat restoration planning and hopes for a cultural center. That work joins care for the river landscape with remembrance of the 1851 negotiations. [17]
Timeline
Dates before the nineteenth century are sometimes approximate. Events concerning the wider Chinookan region are identified where necessary. The source numbers refer to the list that follows.

blocks.text: Crazy Snake Rebellion of 1909
Muscogee resistance to allotment in Oklahoma

The Crazy Snake Rebellion was a brief violent crisis near Henryetta, Oklahoma, in March 1909. It grew out of a longer struggle over Muscogee land and self-government. This account explains the land dispute, Harjo's position and the events of 1909. [2, 5, 8]
The land dispute behind the crisis

The Muscogee people, commonly called the Creeks in older records, had been forced from their southeastern homeland to Indian Territory in the 1830s. Their western home was in what became Oklahoma. Land there supported their families and the tribal towns that organized much of their public and ceremonial life. The dispute over allotment therefore involved control of a country and its institutions as well as ownership of farms. [1, 2]

Article 14 of the Treaty of March 24, 1832, guaranteed the Creek country west of the Mississippi and promised protection against state or territorial laws governing the Creeks. It also allowed them to govern themselves, subject to the general authority Congress might exercise. That qualification matters, but the promise of a protected homeland explains why later federal policies seemed to Harjo and his followers to break an agreement. The treaty itself also ceded the Creeks' eastern lands. [1]
Allotment and federal pressure

Allotment meant dividing land held by a tribal nation into parcels assigned to individuals. Federal officials promoted it as a way to make Native people adopt private farming and American social practices. Economic interests also wanted access to valuable land. For opponents, the change weakened shared landholding and the authority of their own communities. [2]

The Dawes Act of 1887 initially exempted the Muscogee and the other nations known in federal records as the Five Civilized Tribes. Congress created the Dawes Commission in 1893 to negotiate changes with them. The Curtis Act of June 28, 1898, allowed enrollment and allotment to proceed without tribal consent. Later agreements modified the process, but the pressure to divide tribal land continued. Opposition within the Muscogee Nation was not uniform: some leaders negotiated with federal officials while others refused to cooperate. [2, 3]
Chitto Harjo and the earlier resistance

Chitto Harjo was born in 1846 in Indian Territory. His name became widely known in English as Crazy Snake. The name was a loose translation; Harjo carried a meaning associated with reckless bravery. It should not be treated as a medical description. His followers became known as the Snakes. [5]

Hickory Ground near Henryetta became a center of resistance. Harjo served as a spokesman for its leader, Lahtah Micco, and outsiders came to identify the movement especially with him. The Snakes established a rival government intended to preserve older Muscogee laws and customs. Their resistance also included pressure on tribal members who accepted allotment, which brought them into conflict with the recognized Creek National Council. [4]

In January 1901 federal cavalry arrived near Henryetta, but Harjo's arrest on January 27 was peaceful. Authorities prosecuted members of the movement. Further arrests in 1902 led to imprisonment at Leavenworth. After his release, Harjo also used political campaigns and appeals to officials to pursue his aims. These earlier events should be distinguished from the shootings of March 1909. [2, 4]
The treaty argument made by Harjo

Harjo explained his position to a special Senate investigating committee at Tulsa in November 1906. He believed the United States had promised a lasting agreement and that his people had honored their part. His argument rested on an obligation he expected the government to keep. It helps explain why accepting an individual allotment did not settle the larger issue for him. [2, 6]

A translated passage from his testimony, reproduced in a 2025 Oklahoma Supreme Court concurrence, states: “The grass is growing, the waters run, the sun shines, the light is with us, and the agreement is with us yet.” The surviving English wording comes through translation and later reproduction. It gives evidence of Harjo's understanding of the agreement rather than a complete legal account of every treaty provision. [6]
The shootings in March 1909

On March 24 deputies investigated an alleged theft of smoked meat at a Black encampment near Hickory Ground. They returned with a posse on March 25. Shooting left one confirmed Black death and forty-two arrests. Harjo was absent. The accusation supplied the name Smoked Meat Rebellion. [7]

On March 27 a posse attempted to arrest Harjo at his home. Officers Herman Odom and Edward Baum were killed and Harjo was wounded. He escaped. Governor Charles N. Haskell ordered five companies of state militia into the area on March 28 under Colonel Roy V. Hoffman. Posses and vigilantes burned homes and the Snake council house and looted property. Hoffman later reported that fears of large armed bands were unfounded. His assessment confirmed three deaths across the two shootings. [7]
Newspaper reports and historical evidence

News reports could make readers picture a much larger conflict. On March 30, 1909, the Roseburg Review in Oregon described Harjo as surrounded by eight hundred men and seeking surrender terms. That report is useful evidence of the story circulating at the time. It does not establish that every claimed movement or encounter occurred. Harjo was not captured. Comparing the newspaper with later accounts shows why contemporary reports require careful checking. [5, 8]
The name of the conflict can obscure the Black residents in the first encounter. Examining the two shootings separately gives a clearer account of who was involved.
The escape of Harjo and survival of the movement

Harjo went into hiding after being wounded. The Oklahoma Historical Society places his death around 1911 in the Kiamichi Mountains and attributes it to his wound. The approximate date reflects uncertainty surrounding his final years. [5]

The resistance did not simply vanish with Harjo. Appeals for restoration of treaty rights continued for years. His supporters' political work helped sustain later forms of collective activism. The immediate crisis ended without reversing allotment, but Harjo remained a figure through whom Muscogee people remembered their defense of land and self-government. [4, 5]

Historian Donald L. Fixico presents Harjo as a Native patriot defending traditional community life against forced allotment. That interpretation helps explain the distance between Harjo's purposes and the image of a dangerous rebel promoted by some outsiders. It also keeps the land dispute connected to the community traditions that the movement sought to protect. [9]
Place in a chronology of American conflicts
For a chronology of American conflicts, this episode is best classified as a domestic disturbance involving Oklahoma state forces. Federal cavalry appeared in the earlier 1901 episode. [4, 7]

title: Crow War of 1887
contextNote: A historical conflict and its aftermath within the wider history of the Crow people.

blocks.text: Crow War of 1887

The Crow War was a brief armed conflict on the Crow Reservation in Montana Territory. The crisis grew from a horse raid and a confrontation with federal officials, then ended with fighting near Crow Agency on November 5, 1887. Sword Bearer led a Crow faction whose resistance exposed deep tensions within reservation life. The Crow Nation did not act as a united army against the United States. [1–5]

rows: Item
Details
Other names
Sword Bearer Incident, Crow uprising and Wraps Up His Tail uprising
Core dates
September 30 to November 5, 1887
Location
Crow Reservation and Little Bighorn River area in southeastern Montana Territory
Main figures
Sword Bearer; agent Henry E. Williamson; General Thomas H. Ruger; Colonel Nathan A. M. Dudley
Outcome
Federal suppression of the faction; Sword Bearer killed; prisoners removed to Fort Snelling

blocks.text: The dates above describe the main crisis. Military movements and the treatment of prisoners continued afterward. [4, 5, 8–10]
Crow relations with the United States

Crow leaders had often cooperated with the United States to defend their homeland against rival Plains peoples. Crow warriors helped the Army in 1876, including at the Battle of the Rosebud. Their alliance served Crow interests, especially the protection of land and communities. It did not mean that federal demands always matched what Crow people wanted. [2]

The treaty signed with the Crow at Fort Laramie on May 7, 1868, promised peace and established a reservation. It also provided for a resident agent, schools and agricultural support. Article 1 required the surrender of people accused of certain wrongs, while Article 4 preserved a conditional right to hunt beyond the reservation. These terms help explain the later dispute over raiding and federal authority. They do not, by themselves, prove that officials handled the 1887 crisis fairly. [1]
Reservation pressures and Sword Bearer

By the early 1880s, buffalo had disappeared from the Yellowstone Valley. Illness, drought and harsh winters added to the hardships of reservation life. Federal officials pushed farming and other changes. Plenty Coups viewed crops and cattle as ways to preserve his people and homeland, but the loss of older ways of life left some young men dissatisfied. [2, 7]

Sword Bearer was also known as Wraps Up His Tail. In an account published in 1896, Smithsonian ethnologist James Mooney linked his rise to participation in a Cheyenne Sun Dance in 1887 and the gift of a red-painted ceremonial saber. Mooney reported that Sword Bearer claimed protection from bullets. His religious standing helped give his leadership force. [3]

Mooney suggested that Sword Bearer offered followers religious deliverance, but he acknowledged that official records did not clearly establish that teaching. His wider religious message remains uncertain. [3]
The confrontation on September 30

On September 30, a Crow raiding party returned with horses taken from the Piegan, a Blackfeet people. Williamson’s October 1 letter reported that about twenty men returned and that six fired into agency buildings. He requested troops from Fort Custer and pressed for arrests when the raiders resisted. [4]

Williamson described the shooting as unprovoked. His letter is valuable evidence of what he reported and why he requested force, but it gives the agent’s account rather than the raiders’ explanation. The dispute had moved beyond a horse raid into a direct challenge to reservation authority. [4]
The fighting on November 5

The crisis continued for several weeks. On November 4, Dudley moved from Fort Custer with six troops of the 1st Cavalry, infantry and Hotchkiss guns. General Ruger directed the broader operation. The following day, the Army demanded the surrender of the men it wanted and allowed ninety minutes for compliance. [4, 5]

Captain R. P. Page Wainwright’s regimental history states that soldiers advanced after the deadline and that roughly 120 to 150 Crow warriors rode out. The cavalry repulsed their movement, after which the Crow used timber and rifle pits along the river. A troop of the 7th Cavalry operated on the Army’s right. The account reports that fighting stopped soon after Sword Bearer fell. The cavalry returned to Fort Custer on November 13. [5]

Wainwright’s account explains the Army’s movements, but it was written from the regiment’s viewpoint. Its description should be read beside Crow historical evidence rather than treated as the complete story. [5, 6]
Sword Bearer was killed and losses remain disputed

Little Big Horn College’s finding aid for historian Don Rickey’s papers gives a more specific account of Sword Bearer’s death. It states that he was wounded in the skirmish, went to the Little Bighorn River and was shot in the head by Fire Bear, an agency policeman, while kneeling for water. This differs from a simple account in which Army gunfire alone killed him. The finding aid summarizes research material rather than reproducing every underlying witness statement. [6]

The overall death toll is less certain. An American Historical Association report on the 1987 scholarly commemoration identifies Sword Bearer as the only fatality and notes other wounded people. Wainwright’s older military history refers to men killed without giving a reliable complete tally. These accounts do not support presenting one exact casualty total as settled. Sword Bearer’s death is firmly documented; the wider totals require caution. [5, 7]
Prisoners and the families left behind

The National Archives identifies eight Crow prisoners sent to Fort Snelling in Minnesota. In council on December 31, 1887, Plenty Coups asked that they return to help their families farm and tend cattle. He questioned the seriousness of their alleged wrongdoing. [4]

The imprisonment led into the federal boarding school system. A May 1888 War Department record documents the approved transfer of Crow prisoners from Fort Snelling to Carlisle Indian School in Pennsylvania. The surviving copy records communication with Richard Henry Pratt and approval by the Secretary of War. This was an official transfer of prisoners, not simply ordinary school enrollment. [8]

The records also show that returning home could take years. Correspondence from March and April 1890 discusses sending Big Hail, also recorded as Egbert B. Hail, and Theron Lears back to Crow Agency. Carlisle official Alfred John Standing described them as prisoners treated as students and said he did not object to their return. His description reflects the institution’s own position. [9]

On July 1, 1890, Pratt sought permission to use Montana treaty funds to pay for their journey home. The letter documents a request for travel money; it does not by itself establish their actual departure date. The paper trail shows how military detention, schooling and control over travel became connected. [10]
What the conflict reveals

The Crow War shows divisions over how to survive under federal control. Some leaders pursued negotiation and farming. Sword Bearer’s followers challenged the limits of reservation life. Crow police also participated in the suppression of the faction. These roles make a description of the entire Crow people fighting as one force misleading. [2, 4, 6]

The military result was the defeat of Sword Bearer’s movement and the removal of prisoners. Its wider meaning lies in the power federal officials exercised over movement, punishment and family life, even among people who had cooperated with the Army. That conclusion draws on the treaty, military account and later transfer records together. [1, 5, 8–10]

Crow voices remain central to remembering the event. At the 1987 centennial, tribal historian Joe Medicine Crow discussed interviews he had conducted with participants. The commemoration included a marker and an honor song for Wraps His Tail. Little Big Horn College preserves Rickey’s research collection, including oral history transcripts and archival records. These materials help historians compare official descriptions with Crow memories. [6, 7]

title: Klickitat involvement in the wars of 1855 and 1856
contextNote: Queued with Yakama for the confederation and regional context. Klickitat, Cascade, Nisqually, and Yakama identities are not interchangeable; a distinct Klickitat access point remains a research task.

blocks.text: Klickitat War 1855 to 1856
Historical overview and sources

The Klickitat War of 1855–1856 is best understood as Klickitat participation in the wider wars over land and reservations in the Pacific Northwest. The fighting overlapped with the Yakama War east of the Cascade Mountains, the Puget Sound War west of the mountains and the March 1856 attack at the Cascades of the Columbia River. Treating these events as connected gives a clearer account than presenting the Klickitat War as a fully separate conflict. [1, 2, 3]

The Klickitat were a Sahaptin-speaking people whose traditional homeland lay north of the Columbia River, in areas now within Klickitat, Skamania and Clark counties in Washington. During the early nineteenth century, some Klickitat bands moved into western Oregon. They became important traders between communities, dealing in horses, weapons, hides and other goods. [4]

As American settlement grew, Native access to land and food became harder to maintain. In western Oregon, settlers fenced prairies and treated movement across claimed land as trespass. Federal officials promoted reservations as a way to protect Native people while opening much larger areas to settlement. These policies threatened communities’ homes, hunting grounds, fishing places and freedom of movement. [4, 5]

The June 1855 treaty came before the main fighting. At the Walla Walla council, Governor Isaac Stevens and Indian superintendent Joel Palmer pressed tribal leaders to surrender large areas of land. Kamiakin, a leading Yakama chief, opposed the proposed terms before eventually signing. The council brought together peoples with different leaders and interests, so a signature did not mean that every affected community accepted the agreement. [1]

The Treaty with the Yakama, signed June 9, 1855, specifically included the “Klikatat.” It grouped fourteen tribes and bands together under the name Yakama and established a reservation. It also reserved fishing rights at customary places and rights to hunt, gather food and pasture livestock on open and unclaimed land. Its terms required relocation within one year after ratification, which did not occur until 1859. Those dates matter because the treaty should not be described as a surrender that ended the fighting in 1855. [6, 1]

In August 1855, officials forcibly removed several hundred Klickitat people from Oregon to a temporary reserve near present-day White Salmon, Washington. Some had lived in Oregon for years and considered it home. The Oregon Encyclopedia identifies displaced Oregon Klickitats as an important part of the resistance associated with Kamiakin in 1856, including attacks along the Columbia River and lower Lewis River. Removal was therefore one of the direct links between government policy and armed resistance. [4]
The main sequence was:

rows: Date
Event
June 9, 1855
The Treaty with the Yakama included the Klickitat among its participating tribes and bands. [6]
August 1855
Several hundred Klickitat people were removed from Oregon to Washington. [4]
September 1855
Yakama warriors killed Indian agent Andrew J. Bolon amid escalating violence involving miners and Native people. The Army prepared a military response. [7]
October 5, 1855
Yakama forces defeated Major Granville Haller’s troops at Toppenish Creek, beginning the main Yakama War fighting. [7]
Late October 1855
Nisqually and Klickitat fighters clashed with territorial volunteers in the Puget Sound region. Muckleshoot and Klickitat attackers also killed nine settlers along the White River. [2]
January 26, 1856

Native forces attacked Seattle. Gunfire from USS Decatur helped defend the settlement. Territorial officials associated the attack with leaders including Owhi, although accounts of responsibility require care. [8]
Yakama, Klickitat and Cascade fighters attacked settlements and military positions at the Columbia River Cascades. Army reinforcements recovered the area. [3]

blocks.text: The Cascades attack was a struggle over a vital transportation route and fishing area. The river’s dangerous rapids forced travelers to carry goods around them, a process called portaging. Whoever controlled that passage could influence trade and military movement between the lower Columbia and the interior. The area also supported important Native salmon fisheries. Attacking its blockhouses, supplies, transportation facilities and steamers offered a way to interrupt American military operations farther east. [9, 3]

On March 26, attackers struck the Upper, Middle and Lower Cascades. Some settlers took refuge in a military blockhouse while others sheltered in the Bradford brothers’ store. Attackers burned buildings and tried to set the store on fire. The steamers Mary and Wasco escaped upriver, allowing word of the attack to reach Army forces. [3]

HistoryLink reports fourteen civilians and three soldiers killed. The National Park Service’s scholarly study also gives seventeen white deaths, while stressing that Native casualties were poorly recorded. That uneven record makes a complete casualty total difficult to establish. The event became widely known as the Cascades Massacre, a name that emphasizes the deaths of settlers and soldiers. [3, 9]

Lieutenant Philip Sheridan brought reinforcements from Fort Vancouver, while troops under George Wright and Edward Steptoe approached from upriver. The relief forces broke the attack. Sheridan then captured a nearby Cascade community, including men, women and children. The Cascade people were a distinct community, so these prisoners should not simply be described as captured Klickitat fighters. [10, 4]

Sheridan’s later memoir reports that Wright’s military commission sentenced nine Cascade prisoners to death and had them hanged. Sheridan described the prisoners initially denying participation, then treated residue in their gun barrels as evidence of guilt. He also repeated reports of confessions before execution, although he acknowledged that he did not witness the hangings. A cautious reading is that recently fired weapons alone cannot establish which individuals attacked civilians. His memoir provides valuable testimony, but it also defends his own actions and those of the Army. [11]

Violence also reached Native families who had supported American forces. Sheridan described finding the murdered wife and six children of Spencer, a Chinook interpreter working with Wright. He attributed their deaths to white men seeking revenge and condemned the killing of people who had no part in the attack. This account shows how retaliation endangered people regardless of their actual role in the fighting. [11]

The fighting in 1856 did not mark the end of the wider regional war. Resistance and Army campaigns continued, with major defeats of Native forces in 1858. Kamiakin attempted to maintain an alliance across tribal boundaries, but that alliance faced military pressure and internal disagreements. There was no single Native army representing every Klickitat, Yakama or neighboring community. [12]

The lasting consequences included displacement, greater American control over transportation routes and reduced Native control of land and resources. Klickitat people nevertheless remained part of the region. Most descendants of Oregon Klickitats are enrolled in the Yakama Nation, while others have connections to Grand Ronde and Cowlitz communities. Klickitat are among the fourteen tribes and bands represented within the Yakama confederation today. [4, 13]
A precise chronological entry is:
1855–1856: Klickitat involvement in the Yakama and Puget Sound wars, including the March 1856 Cascades attack.
