title: Klamath and Salmon River War of 1855 and its aftermath
contextNote: A regional historical topic linked here for Karuk, Yurok, and Hupa context. The Klamath River is a place name here; this is not a study of the Klamath people of Oregon. Relevance must be assessed source by source.

blocks.text: Klamath and Salmon River War1855 to 1856
The Red Cap War and its aftermath in northwestern California

The Klamath and Salmon River War, also called the Red Cap War, grew out of the California Gold Rush and the struggle over Native homelands in northwestern California. In 1855, miners tried to disarm local Native people. Some resisted, while others surrendered their weapons or sought protection. Volunteer forces attacked villages, Native fighters attacked miners and the U.S. Army intervened. The conflict ended with the defeat or surrender of much of the armed resistance and plans to concentrate Native people on a lower Klamath River reservation. [1; 2; 6]

The main war occurred in 1855. Its effects continued through 1856 and much longer. This account covers the causes, the fighting, efforts to make peace and the reservation system that followed. It also explains why reports written by settlers and government officers require careful reading.
The dates and the name of the war

Many short timelines list the fighting as January through March 1855. Longer accounts show that the settlement took more time. Anthony Jennings Bledsoe describes an April council, continued military activity and an announcement that the war had ended by June 1. National Park Service historian Edwin C. Bearss, using government correspondence, places most Red Cap surrenders by mid-June. Early 1855 through June is therefore a useful range for the main conflict and its settlement. The year 1856 belongs chiefly to the aftermath. [1, pp. 72–77; 2, pp. 174–176]

The word Klamath can cause confusion. This war took place along the Klamath River and its Salmon River tributary in California. It was centered in Yurok and Karuk country. It should be kept separate from the history of the Klamath people and their reservation in southern Oregon. The neighboring Rogue River wars also had their own course, even though unrest on one side of the California and Oregon border affected the other. [1, pp. 72–82; 11, p. 61]
The rivers and the Native communities

The lower Klamath was Yurok homeland, while Karuk communities lived farther upriver and along the middle river. The Salmon River enters the Klamath upstream from Weitchpec, where the Trinity River joins it. These connected waterways linked villages, fishing grounds and trading routes. Salmon provided an important food supply, and river travel by canoe connected communities in country where mountain trails were difficult. [1, pp. 77–78; 2, pp. 153–154]

The Red Caps were a group of resistance fighters associated with more than one Native community. The name should not be treated as the name of a separate tribe or as a label for every Yurok or Karuk person. The Yurok Tribe's own history describes a mixed group whose resistance nearly stopped the settlement effort. Many other Native people sought peace, tried to remain in their villages or made agreements with Army officers. [9; 6]

Local decisions mattered. Villages and families did not all follow one leader or one plan. Hupa communities in nearby Hoopa Valley also faced settler pressure. Scholarship describes some Hupa support for resistance, while older accounts record offers by other Native groups to help arrange surrender. These different responses show why a simple story of two united sides misses much of what happened. [2, pp. 172–174; 11, p. 74]
How the Gold Rush changed the region

The discovery of gold brought miners, merchants and pack trains into lands that Native people already used and governed. Early contact included trade and cooperation. Yurok people transported goods by canoe, and some settlers depended on that help. Relations worsened as newcomers occupied village sites and fishing places and treated Native land as open for their own use. The Yurok Tribe records village destruction and heavy losses from violence and disease during the broader Gold Rush era. Those losses should not all be counted as deaths in this one war. [7]

Mining created a struggle over access. Miners needed river bars, trails and supplies. Native families needed the same river system for food and travel. A village beside the river could stand near a route that miners considered essential. When threats and killings disrupted those routes, traders and miners pressed officials to secure the country. The resulting military policy was closely tied to keeping the mining economy open. [1, pp. 73–75; 2, pp. 169–171]
Failed treaties and unequal protection

Federal agent Redick McKee negotiated with Native communities in 1851. Such agreements offered a way to reduce violence by defining land and promising protection. Settlers objected that the proposed reservations gave Native people too much useful land. The U.S. Senate rejected the eighteen California treaties in 1852, and the treaties remained secret for decades. The Yurok Tribe records that Native communities were not told of the rejection. Promised security therefore failed to become a reliable barrier against settlement. [3, pp. 23–24; 8]

California law also placed Native people at a serious disadvantage. The 1850 Act for the Government and Protection of Indians allowed forms of compulsory labor and restricted Native testimony against white defendants. A 1855 amendment changed the witness rule in cases under that act, but wider exclusions remained a problem. The state also supported armed expeditions against Native people. These policies made it difficult for families to obtain protection when settlers harmed them. [3, pp. 5–8, 15–19]

The failure of these protections helps explain why a demand to hand over weapons could seem dangerous. People who had seen attacks on villages had little reason to assume that disarmament would make them safe. That concern was later confirmed by an Army report describing threats against Native people who had already surrendered their arms. [6]
The crisis in late 1854

A contemporary newspaper offers an important account of the immediate dispute. On February 3, 1855, the Weekly Humboldt Times reported that around December 10 a white man had attempted a sexual assault on a Native woman and had fatally shot her Native companion. It said Native people then killed an ox formerly owned by the accused man. After learning that the animal had changed owners, they offered payment, which was refused. The paper linked this dispute to efforts to disarm Native people and to the burning of villages and winter food supplies. [5]

This was a published allegation, not a court finding. The newspaper acknowledged that the accused man and his friends disputed its report and invited evidence against the charge. It also supported removal to reservations and further military pressure. Its account therefore exposes settler violence while still accepting coercion against Native communities as a solution. [5]

Other violence was occurring near Crescent City, Smith River and Lake Earl, involving Tolowa and neighboring communities. These events helped spread fear through the region. They belong to the wider setting, but their casualties should not automatically be added to a total for the Klamath and Salmon River campaign. [1, pp. 70–72]
The miners demand disarmament

On January 6, 1855, settlers met at Orleans Bar. Their resolutions appeared in the Weekly Humboldt Times on January 13. They pledged to stop the sale, gift, loan or repair of firearms and the supply of ammunition to Native people. They threatened offenders with a shaved head, twenty-five lashes and expulsion from the river. They also claimed authority to seize and sell an offender's property when public officials were absent. [4]

The published resolutions show settlers taking enforcement into their own hands. Bledsoe's later account describes a further demand that nearby Native people surrender weapons by January 19, with death threatened for those who continued to carry them. Some complied. Others, including Red Cap fighters, refused. [2, pp. 164–165]

According to Bledsoe, a party of miners went to a Red Cap village on January 19 and demanded surrender. Defensive gunfire killed William Wheeler and Thomas O'Neil and wounded others. The miners retreated and requested help from Fort Humboldt. This encounter helped turn the dispute over weapons into a wider armed campaign. The date and names come from Bledsoe's later narrative and should be read with that limit in mind. [2, p. 165]
The fighting spreads

Army commander R. C. Buchanan sent Captain Henry M. Judah from Fort Humboldt. Volunteer companies also formed among settlers and miners. These forces did not share one steady command. Men argued over tactics, protection for peaceful villages and whether the state would pay their expenses. The term militia can hide these differences: local armed parties and federal regulars did not always act together or have the same aims. [2, pp. 166–174]

Some miners wanted to attack Native communities regardless of whether they had taken part in the fighting. Others objected. Bledsoe records Salmon River miners resisting plans for a general massacre. Meanwhile, Red Cap fighters used the mountains as shelter, and attacks on miners and supply routes made ordinary work difficult. Burning villages could drive people who had sought peace into the hills and widen the resistance. [2, pp. 166–171]

One major episode occurred in early February around villages called Cappell and Moreo in older records. Bledsoe describes an encounter on February 4 followed by volunteer attacks the next day. He reports twenty-six Native people killed and twenty-three captured in the two village attacks. He calls the dead warriors, but his account does not establish the role of every person killed. The figures are reported counts from a later settler history, not a complete or independently verified casualty list. [2, pp. 168–169]

Attacks also struck people who had been promised safety. Bearss, drawing on Army correspondence, describes volunteers calling Yurok people out of a village, shaking hands with them and then opening fire. Women were taken away as prisoners. Such incidents damaged the credibility of promises that surrender would bring protection. [1, pp. 75–76]
What the Army reported

General John E. Wool's February 26, 1855 letter provides a contemporary view of the crisis. He reported that some settlers had organized to destroy peaceful Native people who had given up their weapons under a promise of safety. Judah chose to protect those communities rather than leave them exposed while he pursued fighters in the mountains. Wool also reported that Judah returned to Fort Humboldt on February 7 because Buchanan could not supply him during the winter. [6]

This supply problem gives a more specific explanation than Bledsoe's later attack on Buchanan's indecision. Wool further complained that local civil authority was absent and that courts acquitted offenders in cases involving attacks on Native people. His letter shows divisions among settlers and describes an Army effort to prevent mass killing. It remains an official account of the Army's own conduct, so it should be compared with other evidence. [6; 2, pp. 167–171]

Protection by the Army still operated within a policy of U.S. control. Federal officers and Indian agents sought surrender, punishment of selected fighters and reservation settlement. Their intervention could restrain volunteer violence while also narrowing Native freedom to remain armed and live where they chose. [1, pp. 76–81]
How the war ended

Peace depended partly on Native diplomacy. Communities used messengers to carry proposals between villages. Some offered to help secure the surrender of Red Cap fighters if their own families and property received protection. Settler threats and disagreements among volunteer commanders disrupted these plans. Native cooperation was therefore a calculated effort to survive a dangerous situation. [2, pp. 172–174]

Judah returned to the Klamath in March. In early April, councils brought together representatives of local communities. Bearss describes an agreement to pursue selected Red Cap fighters accused of killing settlers and to encourage others to surrender. Food and weapons would be supplied to Native men assisting the operation. The arrangement combined negotiation with threats of execution and continued military pressure. [1, pp. 75–77]

Bledsoe describes Judah dismissing divided volunteer companies and later being replaced by Captain DeLancey Floyd-Jones. Special agent S. G. Whipple helped organize the settlement and proposed concentrating Native people along the lower river. By June, several resistance leaders had died and most followers had surrendered. Some remained in the mountains. The main campaign ended through a mixture of exhaustion, pressure and agreements, rather than one decisive battlefield victory. [1, pp. 77–79; 2, pp. 174–176]
The reservation established in November 1855

The end of the main fighting and the legal creation of the reservation were separate events. On November 16, 1855, President Franklin Pierce approved the Klamath River Reservation. It ran approximately twenty miles upstream from the Pacific Ocean and extended one mile on each side of the river. The authorized area could not exceed 25,000 acres. The presidential date and boundaries are confirmed in the later Supreme Court decision Mattz v. Arnett. A March 1855 congressional funding law should not be confused with the November order establishing this particular reservation. [13]

Whipple had initially proposed a much wider area. Officials reduced the proposal before it received presidential approval. They regarded the river's fish, some cultivable flats and difficult terrain as advantages. They also hoped to concentrate Native people there at low cost. The reserve covered only a limited part of the region's Native homelands. It did not restore the land and security promised in the earlier treaty process. [1, pp. 77–81]

For some Yurok families, a lower river reservation allowed continued residence within part of their homeland. It also imposed confinement and federal supervision. The Yurok Tribe's account emphasizes the hardship created by a reserve much smaller than its ancestral territory and the later pressure to adopt farming and English. It is misleading to describe reservation life simply as a welcome or easy outcome. [10]
The aftermath during 1856 and beyond

In 1856, the government sought to develop gardens and potato crops on the reservation and supplied tools, seeds and materials for fishing nets. Troops helped maintain control. Whipple resigned that year and was replaced by James A. Patterson. Bearss records disputes over promises of support and compensation to Tolowa people whom officials tried to settle in the lower river area. Their return to their own communities shows the limits of the government's effort to concentrate different peoples in one place. [1, pp. 81–83]

Violence elsewhere on the Klamath also continued. Historian Tara Aine Keegan, drawing on Benjamin Madley's research, identifies two attacks on Karuk people in April 1856, including one near Happy Camp on April 20. She reports at least seventeen people killed across those attacks. These belong to the continuing violence after the main Red Cap campaign. They do not establish that one unchanged war ran continuously through all of 1856. [11, pp. 61–62]

The later history also included survival and continued attachment to the river. Flooding in the winter of 1861 and 1862 damaged reservation facilities and prompted efforts to move residents. Many Yurok people remained or returned. In 1973, the Supreme Court held in Mattz v. Arnett that the reservation had not been terminated by the 1892 law opening land to settlement. The Court left the particular fishing rights questions in that case for further proceedings. The ruling helps show how the land arrangements made after the war continued to matter. [10; 13]
Casualties and the limits of the evidence

The sources used here do not support one reliable total for everyone killed in the war. They record particular attacks and deaths, but often mix armed fighters with village residents. They also sometimes combine the Klamath campaign with violence near Crescent City or with later attacks farther upriver. A careful account should keep those events separate and avoid converting regional population losses into a battlefield death toll. [1; 2; 7]

Bledsoe wrote in 1885, about thirty years after the events. He preserved valuable details but used racial stereotypes and sometimes made clear mistakes. On page 168, he places Ulysses S. Grant at the mouth of the Salmon during the 1855 conflict. Grant had already resigned from the Army in 1854, effective July 31. That episode cannot be accepted as an accurate account of Grant's service. His error is a reason to cross-check the book's names, dates and claims. [2; 14]

Government reports also had purposes. Officers defended decisions, agents requested funds and settlers argued for protection or reimbursement. Native people's views often reach the written record through those outsiders. Official Yurok histories and modern scholarship help restore a perspective that many nineteenth-century accounts minimized.
Why the war matters in American history

The Klamath and Salmon River War shows how conquest could happen through local demands, armed volunteer activity and federal policy working in the same place. Settlers claimed control over weapons and land. Native communities resisted, sought protection or negotiated under pressure. Officials tried to stop some killings while building a reservation system that restricted Native independence.

Historians place this conflict within the wider California genocide. Benjamin Madley identifies deliberate killing, forced confinement and unfree labor as major causes of Native losses under U.S. rule, alongside disease and starvation. Here, contemporary evidence is especially important: a local newspaper acknowledged settler responsibility, and an Army commander reported plans to destroy people who had already disarmed. These records support the term genocide for the wider campaign of destruction without requiring us to treat every settler or soldier as having the same aim. [5; 6; 12]

The return of mining did not settle the underlying questions of Native land, safety and control of the river. The 1855 reservation reduced some immediate conflict while leaving families to face continued violence and outside supervision. Their continued presence along the Klamath is part of the war's history as much as the fighting itself. [1; 10; 13]

blocks.text: Tecumseh and Tippecanoe 1811 to 1813
Origins battles and consequences

Tecumseh's War was a struggle over Native land and political independence in the Old Northwest, the region around the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. Tecumseh and his younger brother Tenskwatawa built an alliance to resist American expansion. William Henry Harrison, governor of Indiana Territory, worked to open more land to American settlement. Their conflict produced the Battle of Tippecanoe on November 7, 1811 and later became part of the War of 1812. Tecumseh's death at the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813 dealt the alliance a major blow. [1, 4, 15]

The dates 1811 to 1813 identify the main military phase of this struggle. Its roots reached back much earlier, and its consequences lasted far longer. Tippecanoe damaged the movement, but it did not end it. Tecumseh was away during that battle. He continued fighting and helped the British capture Detroit in 1812. [1, 14]
Land and the earlier wars

The American Revolution did not settle who would control the Ohio Valley. American leaders claimed western territory while Native nations continued to occupy and defend it. An earlier Native alliance resisted American armies during the Northwest Indian War. Its defeat at Fallen Timbers in 1794 led to the Treaty of Greenville in 1795, through which Native signers gave up most of present-day Ohio. Tecumseh had fought in that earlier struggle. [1]

The loss of land had consequences beyond a change on a map. It threatened hunting grounds, farms and the ability of communities to support themselves. Tecumseh believed that separate treaties allowed Americans to take Native territory a piece at a time. He sought a broader alliance that could resist this process. His movement grew out of Native efforts to survive American expansion. [1, 8]
Tecumseh Tenskwatawa and Prophetstown

Tecumseh became known as a warrior and speaker who traveled widely to recruit allies. Tenskwatawa supplied the religious message that drew people together. Known to Americans as the Shawnee Prophet, he urged Native people to reject alcohol and practices that he believed weakened their communities. His teachings called for spiritual renewal and greater unity among Native nations. [2, 4]

Tenskwatawa was central to the movement's early growth. R. David Edmunds's scholarly biography, The Shawnee Prophet, challenges the habit of treating him as only Tecumseh's assistant. The publisher's account of the book emphasizes the Prophet's role in creating the beliefs and ceremonies that helped unite followers. Religion gave people a reason to join and remain connected across tribal lines. [3]

In 1808, the brothers established Prophetstown near the meeting of the Wabash and Tippecanoe rivers in present-day Indiana. It became a gathering place for people from several Native nations. Families lived and grew food there while visitors heard Tenskwatawa's teachings. Tecumseh traveled beyond the settlement to expand the alliance. [4, 9]

Unity was difficult. Native nations had their own leaders, land claims and survival plans. Some Miami leaders viewed Prophetstown as a threat to their authority within the Miami homeland. Many wanted to preserve peace with the United States, while some younger men supported the brothers. These divisions show why the movement should not be treated as one army representing every Native community. [5]
The Fort Wayne treaty and failed talks

The Treaty of Fort Wayne, signed on September 30, 1809, sharply increased tensions. Harrison negotiated with representatives of the Delaware, Potawatomi, Miami and Eel River Miami peoples. The land agreement and related arrangements opened roughly three million acres to the United States. The treaty offered goods and yearly payments, called annuities, in return for giving up the land. [6, 7]

The treaty itself shows how complicated Native land rights were. Article II recognized that the Miami and Delaware had equal rights to land watered by the White River and that neither could dispose of it without the other's consent. Article V required Wea consent for one tract. Article IX made another cession depend on Kickapoo agreement. Even this American treaty recognized overlapping interests and the need for consent from more than one community. [6]

Tecumseh rejected the sale. He argued that Native land belonged in common to Native nations and could not be sold without their wider agreement. Harrison continued to recognize the authority of the chiefs who had signed. The dispute concerned who could speak for the land and whose consent mattered. [8]

Tecumseh met Harrison at Vincennes in August 1810 and July 1811. He demanded that the United States respect the alliance's position on land sales. The talks failed to resolve the dispute. Tecumseh also explained that the movement wished to preserve peace but would defend its villages against an American advance. In 1811, he traveled south to seek support among the Creek, Chickasaw and Choctaw peoples. This left Tenskwatawa at Prophetstown when Harrison marched toward it. [4, 8]
Tippecanoe in November 1811
The march and the battle

Harrison moved toward Prophetstown with roughly 900 to 1,000 regular soldiers and militia. On November 6, his army approached the settlement. John Tipton, an Indiana militiaman who kept a campaign journal, recorded that Native representatives asked for peace and promised a further meeting the next morning. Harrison's men then camped nearby. [9]

The troops formed a defensive perimeter. Men slept in their clothes, sentries watched the approaches and campfires provided warmth during the cold night. Before daylight on November 7, warriors associated with Prophetstown attacked. Some American soldiers awoke with attackers already close to their tents. Fighting continued for about two hours before American counterattacks forced the warriors to withdraw. Harrison's army held its camp. [9, 10]

The victory was costly. The Tippecanoe County Historical Association records 37 American soldiers killed during the battle and another 25 who later died of their injuries. More than 100 were wounded. Native losses remain uncertain. Those limits matter when comparing later claims that the battle was an easy or overwhelming victory. [10]
The destruction of Prophetstown

On November 8, American scouts found that most residents had left Prophetstown. Harrison's men burned the settlement and destroyed food supplies. Tipton wrote that soldiers carried away six wagonloads of corn and burned an estimated 2,000 bushels. His estimate is a participant's report, rather than an exact modern count. The destruction deprived displaced families of homes and stored food as winter approached. [9]

Tenskwatawa lost influence after the defeat. Some accounts blamed him for encouraging an attack before the alliance was ready and for promising spiritual protection to the warriors. Yet his following did not disappear. He continued to preach after Tippecanoe and after Tecumseh's death. The defeat weakened his authority without immediately ending the religious movement. [2, 10]

Tippecanoe achieved Harrison's immediate goal of damaging the alliance's main settlement. It also made peace harder. Critics accused Harrison of provoking resistance and pushing Tecumseh toward Britain. Supporters presented the battle as a great American victory. The movement's later successes in 1812 show that destroying Prophetstown had not settled the conflict. [11, 14]
The fighting joins the War of 1812

American officials often claimed that British agents were behind Native resistance. Britain did maintain ties with Native nations and provide weapons and supplies through its Indian Department. These connections were real, but Native communities had their own reasons for resisting American settlement. British officers also urged restraint before Britain and the United States formally went to war. [12]

The United States declared war on Great Britain on June 18, 1812. Maritime disputes, including British interference with American trade and the seizure of sailors for British service, helped cause that wider war. Borderland fighting added to the hostility. Tecumseh's struggle now became part of a larger conflict whose western campaigns overlapped the war that had begun in 1811. [11, 12, 14]

Tecumseh allied with British forces to strengthen the defense of Native land. Britain needed Native allies to help protect Upper Canada, now largely southern Ontario. These goals overlapped, but Britain sought the security of its colony while Tecumseh sought a future for Native nations beyond American control. The alliance depended on continued British military support. [12, 14]

In August 1812, Tecumseh and British Major General Isaac Brock helped force the surrender of Detroit. Native warriors disrupted American supply routes and added to the pressure on General William Hull's command. Hull's fear of the opposing force, reinforced by Brock's threats and artillery fire, helped bring about the surrender. This major victory demonstrated that Native resistance remained militarily powerful after Tippecanoe. [12, 14]

The wider fighting also struck communities that had tried to stay neutral. In December 1812, American troops attacked Miami and Delaware settlements along the Mississinewa River. Homes were burned and civilians were captured. Historians George Ironstrack and Cameron Shriver show that these communities had pursued peace before the attacks. Their account also challenges the later claim that Tecumseh commanded the Native counterattack. Local Miami and Delaware leaders organized it. [13]
The campaigns of 1813 and the Thames

In May 1813, British and Native forces failed to capture Fort Meigs in Ohio. Tecumseh also intervened there to stop the killing of captured American soldiers. The incident shows that Native commanders made their own decisions about the conduct of war. Tecumseh's leadership included attempts to restrain violence against prisoners. [14]

The decisive change came on September 10, 1813, when Oliver Hazard Perry's American fleet defeated the British on Lake Erie. Control of the lake threatened British supply lines and made their positions around Detroit and Amherstburg difficult to hold. British commander Henry Procter retreated into Upper Canada with Native allies. Tecumseh opposed the retreat because it exposed the lands his movement was trying to protect. [14, 15]

Harrison pursued the withdrawing force. On October 5, 1813, the armies met near Moraviantown on the Thames River. American mounted troops broke the British line. Native warriors continued fighting, but the allied force was defeated and Tecumseh was killed. His death removed a leader who had spent years linking distant communities into a common military effort. [15]

The loss at the Thames badly weakened the western alliance. Its members still had their own communities and leaders, but they had lost Tecumseh and dependable support from a British force in the region. The American victory strengthened U.S. control around Detroit. It did not end the entire War of 1812 or all Native resistance. [5, 15, 17]
What defeat changed

Tecumseh's goal of a secure Native homeland remained unrealized. The Treaty of Ghent, signed on December 24, 1814, ended the wider Anglo-American war after ratification in 1815. Article IX required both countries to end hostilities with Native nations and restore the possessions, rights and privileges they had held or been entitled to in 1811, provided those nations also stopped fighting. The treaty did not establish the separate Native state sought by the alliance. [16]

That promise did not provide lasting protection from American expansion. The United States largely ignored the provision, and Britain showed little interest in enforcing it. As American settlement spread, Native nations faced further land loss and pressure to leave their homelands. The peace restored the relationship between the two larger powers without securing Tecumseh's political aims. [17]

Native people nevertheless continued to negotiate and resist. John T. Peyton's study of the Miami shows that they rebuilt political unity after the war and used diplomacy and changing landholding practices to protect part of their homeland. Tecumseh's defeat greatly reduced the strength of one military alliance, but Native nations continued to make choices and defend their interests. [5]
History and later memory

Tippecanoe helped build Harrison's public reputation. In the presidential election of 1840, the slogan Tippecanoe and Tyler Too connected his candidacy to the battle. A costly frontier engagement became a simple political story about a victorious commander. That later image left less room for the disputed treaty, the destruction of food supplies or the alliance's continued fighting. [11]

The sources also require care. The Fort Wayne treaty records an agreement, but it cannot establish that all affected people accepted the sale. Tipton's journal preserves a soldier's view of battle and destruction, not the views of Prophetstown's displaced residents. Modern scholarship and Myaamia historical work help recover differences among Native communities that American military accounts often overlooked. [5, 6, 9, 13]

blocks.text: Tonto Apache
Culture History and Timeline

The Tonto Apache are Native people of central Arizona whose history reaches beyond the boundaries of the modern Payson reservation. This study explains their homeland and daily life, follows the effects of warfare and forced removal and describes the rebuilding of community institutions. Traditional practices discussed here often belong to the wider Western Apache world; local customs vary among families and communities.
Names and homeland

Tonto Apache refers to historic communities within the wider Western Apache world. Scholars commonly distinguish Northern Tonto and Southern Tonto groups. These labels describe patterns of speech, kinship and territory rather than a single government that once ruled every Tonto community. [2]

The modern Tonto Apache Tribe is a federally recognized nation beside Payson in central Arizona. Its community belongs to the Rim Country, where the Mogollon Rim rises above surrounding valleys. The tribe's school identifies the people as Dilzhe'e and stresses that their presence predates the town of Payson. [12]

The Yavapai-Apache Nation in the Verde Valley is another tribal nation with Tonto Apache descendants. It brings together two distinct peoples. Its Apache members identify as Dil'zhe'e and speak an Athabaskan language; its Yavapai members have a language in the Yuman family. Shared history and close community ties do not erase this difference. [1]
Food and seasonal life

Western Apache families moved between elevations as foods became available. Gathering and hunting supplied most food. Acorns, pine nuts, grass seeds, mesquite pods and agave were among the resources used across the wider region. Some communities grew corn, beans and squash, though Northern Tonto groups practiced little farming. Seasonal travel linked familiar places and stored foods. It required close knowledge of plants, water and animal behavior. [2]

A 2025 tree-ring study found evidence of frequent small fires linked to Western Apache burning in central and eastern Arizona. Fire helped manage useful resources. This regional finding does not establish identical practices for every Tonto community. [2]
Families homes and clothing

Extended families formed an important part of Western Apache social life. Kinship often followed the mother's line, a system called matrilineal descent. Relatives shared responsibilities that reached beyond one household. Keith Basso's historical study describes this family structure as continuing despite the disruption of older bands under reservation rule. His detailed fieldwork centered on Cibecue, so local Tonto customs should not be assumed to match every detail. [4]

In the wider Apache region, a traditional dwelling was the wickiup, a dome built from bent poles and covered with grass or other material. Women commonly built and maintained it. These homes suited a life that involved seasonal movement. Hides supplied leather for clothing and containers. Modern Apache people use many kinds of housing and clothing; these older practices describe particular historical settings. [3]
Basketry and other arts

Surviving Tonto Apache objects show how craft joined useful design with knowledge of local materials. The Smithsonian holds a water vessel dated 1900-1919 and collected at Payson in 1919. It combines sumac, leather and pine pitch. The pitch coating helped the woven vessel hold water. The record lists Annie or Lela as possible former owners, preserving a small trace of individual lives behind the object. Their surnames and the maker's identity are not established by the catalog. [5]

A second Smithsonian record documents a Tonto Apache burden basket collected near Payson in 1919. It uses willow and hide thong, joined through twining, stitching and tying. Such a carrying basket belonged to the practical equipment of daily work. The record names Jim, also called Sla-ki, as a possible former owner. Taken together, these objects provide specific evidence of Tonto Apache work beyond broad descriptions of Apache culture. [6]
The University of Arizona's tribal profile also identifies beadwork and basketry as Tonto Apache arts. These arts remain part of the community's public identity. [11]
Music religion and ceremony

Singing carries cultural and religious knowledge in Apache communities. In an oral history recorded by the National Park Service, San Carlos Apache musician Chesley Wilson Sr. describes learning songs by hearing them. He also explains an Apache violin made from an agave stalk with one string. His account illustrates the wider Apache musical world rather than proving that every instrument or song was shared by all Tonto families. [3]

The Sunrise Ceremony marks a girl's passage toward adulthood in Western Apache traditions. Basso's account explains its connection to Changing Woman, a sacred figure associated with renewal and long life. Singing, dancing, relatives and sponsors support the young woman. The ceremony also expresses concern for the wider community's health and well-being. Details vary by place, and Basso's Cibecue account should be read in its historical setting. [4]

The Yavapai-Apache Nation published a family announcement for an Apache Sunrise Ceremony in 2022. This is direct evidence that the tradition continues within a living community. Individual religious lives vary, and some Apache people also practice Christianity. [3, 15]
Conflict and forced removal

Mexico's 1848 cession brought central Arizona under a United States claim. Gold discoveries near Prescott in 1863 accelerated settlement. Newcomers occupied water sources and hunting areas, increasing conflict with local Native communities. [8]

The violence included attacks on civilians. In January 1864, King Woolsey's party killed more than 30 Native people at Bloody Tanks after drawing them to a meeting. The Rio Verde reservation was established in 1871. General George Crook's campaign of 1872-1873 then used mobile troops and Native scouts to pursue communities and destroy camps. Delshay was among the Tonto Apache leaders involved in resistance and surrender. [7]

Older military labels need care. The army described the people attacked at Skeleton Cave in December 1872 as Tonto Apaches. Fort McDowell Yavapai identify the victims as their people. The dead included women and children. Treating all these victims as members of today's Tonto Apache Tribe would repeat the confusion in nineteenth-century records. [7]

Families at Rio Verde developed irrigated farming, but federal officials removed them to San Carlos in 1875. The Yavapai-Apache Nation dates the departure to February 27 and reports more than 100 deaths on the winter march. Accounts differ on the distance traveled. [8]
Return and federal recognition

By the 1890s, families were returning toward the Verde Valley, Tonto Basin and Rim Country. They found many useful lands and water sources occupied by newcomers. Some worked on ranches, in mines or on construction projects. Returning home therefore did not restore their former access to the land. [8]
The Payson community continued seeking a secure land base. Its school credits Chief Milton Campbell with leading the effort for reservation land and federal recognition in the 1970s. [12]

On October 6, 1972, Congress enacted Public Law 92-470. It authorized selection of a village site of no more than 85 acres in Tonto National Forest and declared the selected land held in trust as a reservation. It also recognized the Payson Community of Yavapai-Apache Indians as a tribe under the Indian Reorganization Act. This older legal name refers to the Payson community that became the Tonto Apache Tribe. Recognition in 1972 marks a federal legal milestone in the history of an already existing people. [9]
Government and community today

The tribal constitution's election certificate records adoption on December 22, 1979. It establishes a council with five voting members: a chair, a vice chair and three council members. The constitution gives the tribal government responsibilities that include managing funds, regulating land use and protecting natural resources. It also provides elections and procedures for members to challenge officials. Tribal sovereignty means authority to govern tribal affairs within the legal framework that applies to Native nations. [10]

The University of Arizona describes the Payson reservation as 85 acres, a very small base compared with the people's wider homeland. Its profile lists the tribally operated Mazatzal Hotel and Casino as an important local employer. It reports an estimated 102 residents on the reservation and associated trust land from the 2018-2022 American Community Survey. That dated residence estimate is not a current tribal enrollment total. [11]

The Tonto Apache Community School was established in 2023 under tribal law. It serves primary and elementary education, with an early learning program also developed for younger children. The school describes tribal control over curriculum and cultural teaching as central to its purpose. It gives the community a direct role in deciding how its children learn. [12]
Language teaching and remembrance

Related cultural work continues in the Verde Valley. In April 2026, the Yavapai-Apache Nation's Apache Culture Department reported a class on grammar and use of the Dilzhe'e Apache Learners' Dictionary. Participants practiced pronunciation and learned how to use the dictionary. This belongs to the Yavapai-Apache Nation's language program, which is distinct from the Payson tribe's school. Both examples show communities taking part in cultural education today. [13]

The Yavapai-Apache Nation also commemorates the removal and return through Exodus Day. Its 2026 program scheduled a blessing, a run from San Carlos to Camp Verde and a remembrance march. These activities connect younger people with ancestors and places that remain part of community identity. The history of removal continues to matter in how people remember home and teach their children. [14]

blocks.text: Umatilla Culture History and Timeline
The Umatilla people and the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation

The Umatilla are a Native people of the Columbia Plateau whose history centers on the Columbia River and its tributaries. Today they share a government with the Cayuse and Walla Walla through the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation, commonly called CTUIR. Each people retains a distinct heritage. Their shared government supports a living community with its own political institutions, businesses and cultural programs. [1]

This study follows the Umatilla from their river homeland through treaty making, reservation life and the recovery of greater control over tribal affairs. Food, language and access to land connect these periods. Because many institutions now serve all three peoples, their shared history is identified as CTUIR history where appropriate. [7]

blocks.text: Basic facts about the Umatilla and their shared government

The Umatilla homeland crossed the Columbia rather than stopping at today's Oregon and Washington boundary. Tribal history places Umatilla communities on both sides of the river near the Umatilla River's mouth, extending downstream toward Willow Creek on the Oregon side and Rock Creek on the Washington side. River travel linked families and trading partners across this country. [2]

The reservation is a smaller part of that wider homeland. CTUIR describes it as about 172,000 acres. Reservation boundaries and tribal land ownership are different measures: land inside the reservation includes several ownership categories. The historic territory ceded by the three peoples covered about 6.4 million acres. Those figures concern the confederation as a whole. [3]
Food and the yearly round

Families followed a yearly round of fishing, root digging, berry picking and hunting. Movement depended on when foods became available at different elevations. Harvests were dried and stored so that a productive season could help carry people through winter. Salmon was central, alongside foods such as biscuitroot, berries, deer and elk. [4]

blocks.text: The shared seasonal pattern described by CTUIR [4]

These journeys followed familiar places and recurring tasks. People needed knowledge of fish runs, plants, weather and food storage. A fishing site could also bring people together for trade and family visits. The seasonal pattern connected lowland rivers with upland food sources. [4, 20]
Homes family and material culture

Housing varied across the Columbia Plateau. James Ronda's study of Lewis and Clark describes mat-covered lodges as common between the Snake and Columbia confluence and The Dalles in 1805. Poles supported these buildings, which could shelter many people. His account specifically identifies Umatilla mat houses near the Umatilla River. These lodges were an important part of the river communities' built environment. [5]

Baskets, hats and woven bags could hold food or display designs and symbols. Oral stories, songs and dance preserved family and community histories. Elders taught children through everyday work and guidance. Leaders gained standing through experience, useful skills and the ability to bring people toward agreement in council. [2]

Celilo Falls was one of the great gathering places in the wider river network. People came to fish, exchange goods, take part in ceremonies and visit. Its trading connections placed Umatilla history within a much larger Indigenous economy. [14]
Language and oral knowledge

Umatilla is a southern dialect of Sahaptin. Walla Walla is a different Sahaptin dialect. The original Cayuse language was distinct; the language now taught as Weyíiletpuu is a form of Nez Perce used by Cayuse people. These differences matter because sharing a government does not mean that the three peoples always spoke one language. [6]

CTUIR's language program records speakers, protects language materials and teaches people of different ages. A printed and online Umatilla dictionary gives learners another way to study. The tribal language page explains that language carries community history and ways of understanding the world. Revitalization therefore involves helping people use it as well as preserving written records. [6]
Belief and responsibilities to the land

Some members continue to practice Washat, also called Seven Drums. Other members follow Christian traditions. Religious life within the confederation has changed over time and differs among families. Traditional worship, singing, drumming and food gathering remain part of community life. [3, 7]

Tamánwit refers to traditional law governing proper relationships among people and the surrounding world. At the 1855 council, tribal speakers drew on these relationships when explaining why land could not be treated simply as something to sell. Their arguments connected the earth, ancestors and the foods on which their people depended. [10]

First Foods express a continuing responsibility between people and the sources of life. Water, salmon, game, roots and berries have places in this framework. CTUIR's Umatilla River Vision explains that ceremonial food order recalls the foods' promise to sustain people and people's duty to care for them. This belief also shapes present resource management. [8]
Horses and outside contact

The Umatilla, Cayuse and Walla Walla became known for horsemanship. Horses made it easier to carry goods and travel farther, widening trade and other contacts. Their use became part of an economy that linked fishing and gathering with livestock and exchanges across the region. The river remained important alongside travel over land. [2, 3, 17]

Lewis and Clark passed through this region in 1805 and 1806. Native communities already had fishing grounds, trading connections and geographic knowledge. They supplied food, guidance and opportunities to exchange goods. The expedition entered an established Indigenous world. Encounters differed from village to village, and the explorers' written descriptions reflect their own viewpoint. [5, 20]
Disease missions and settlement

During the nineteenth century, missionaries and settlers brought growing pressure on Plateau communities. The Whitman mission stood in Cayuse country and became an important Oregon Trail stop. Disease, disputes over supplies, religious conflict and increasing settlement damaged relations. A severe measles crisis helped deepen suspicion of Marcus Whitman's medical work. [9]

In November 1847, an attack killed Marcus and Narcissa Whitman and other people at the mission. The resulting Cayuse War and expanding American control affected communities across the wider Plateau. The crisis became one justification for greater settler and government pressure on Native lands. [9]
The Treaty of 1855

United States officials Isaac Stevens and Joel Palmer sought land cessions at the Walla Walla council in 1855. Native leaders attended to protect their people and presented strong objections to surrendering their homelands. Historian Cliff Trafzer describes a negotiation shaped by unequal power and the threat of settler intrusion. Agreement emerged under that pressure. [10]

The Walla Walla, Cayuse and Umatilla treaty was signed on June 9, 1855. It was ratified on March 8, 1859. Article 1 set aside a reservation and reserved fishing rights in reservation waters and at usual and accustomed stations outside it. It also secured hunting, root and berry gathering and livestock grazing on unclaimed lands. These clauses preserved activities beyond the reservation. [11]

The treaty also imposed restrictions and promoted permanent farming. Article 6 allowed individual land assignments and threatened penalties for leaving assigned homes under specified conditions. The same document therefore protected important resource rights while giving federal officials tools to press for a different way of life. Its promises must be distinguished from later government conduct. [11]
Allotment and boarding schools

Allotment meant dividing reservation land into individual parcels. On Umatilla, Congress began this process through the Slater Act of 1885, before the broader General Allotment Act of 1887. Further legislation in 1888 reduced the reservation. Opening land to outsiders and breaking up the reservation estate weakened the land base available to the community. [12]

Schools were another part of federal efforts to replace Native ways of life. Patrick Lozar's University of Oregon thesis documents the Umatilla boarding school completed in 1883. Officials sought to reshape children's clothing, work and daily conduct through close supervision. Boys received agricultural training while girls were taught household work. The purpose extended well beyond teaching reading and writing. [13]

Families and leaders responded in different ways. Some wanted schooling that would help children deal with the changing economy while they challenged church control or sought more influence over education. Umatilla leader Wenap Snoot took part in these negotiations. Lozar calls the broader response adaptive resistance: people sometimes used new institutions while working to preserve family and tribal interests. Acceptance of a useful skill did not necessarily mean agreement with assimilation. [13]
Government and self determination

The adoption of a constitution and bylaws in 1949 established the modern elected government. CTUIR's governing Board of Trustees has nine members, including its chair. The General Council consists of adult tribal members and elects the Board. It also provides a forum where members hear reports and raise concerns. [1]

These institutions let the confederation make decisions about education, natural resources and other public affairs through its own government. Sovereignty means a people's authority to govern itself. Present tribal government draws on the continuing political identity of the peoples whose representatives negotiated the treaty, while using institutions that have changed over time. [1, 10]
Fishing rights and salmon restoration

The flooding of Celilo Falls on March 10, 1957, behind The Dalles Dam destroyed a major fishery and gathering place. The loss damaged an economy built around the river and separated people from an important cultural site. Compensation for inundated fishing places did not purchase or cancel the treaty fishing rights themselves. [14]

Tribal fishers and governments continued to press those rights. In 1969, Judge Robert Belloni's decision in the combined Sohappy v. Smith and United States v. Oregon cases recognized a tribal entitlement to a fair share of fish and limited discriminatory state regulation. In 1977, CTUIR joined three other Columbia Basin tribal governments to create the Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission. [15]

In the Umatilla Basin, irrigation diversions had helped eliminate Chinook runs. Tribally led restoration brought together fish reintroduction, passage improvements and negotiations over water. Congress authorized the Umatilla Basin Project in 1988, and an agreement in 1992 advanced implementation. The water exchange supplied Columbia water to irrigation systems so that more Umatilla River water could remain available to fish. Salmon returned, although harmful water temperatures and low summer flows remained concerns. [16]

The River Vision connects restoration with First Foods. It treats a healthy river as a functioning system of water flows, floodplains, plants and aquatic life. Success includes whether that system can continue to provide foods important to the tribal community. The approach brings cultural knowledge into direct conversation with river science and habitat management. [8]
Umatilla life today

The confederation's economy includes farming, livestock, timber and commercial enterprises. Wildhorse Resort and Casino and Cayuse Technologies are examples of businesses developed under tribal ownership. Cayuse Technologies opened on the reservation in 2006. These activities exist alongside the continuing importance of fishing, hunting and gathering. [17]

Tamástslikt Cultural Institute presents the history of the Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla from a tribal perspective. Its exhibits connect western expansion and its effects with present community life and future concerns. The institute helps the peoples explain their history publicly in their own terms. [18]

Education is also part of cultural continuity. CTUIR's education program explicitly connects learning with language, traditional foods, family and tribal sovereignty. It calls for children to encounter food traditions and stories at school and at home. This places the transmission of knowledge within everyday education. [19]

Umatilla history continues in decisions about rivers, schools and the use of land. Maintaining cultural knowledge depends partly on having places where people can practice it and institutions through which they can protect those places. The connection between food traditions and present government remains visible in both education and environmental work. [8, 19]

blocks.text: Walla Walla History Culture and Timeline
Who the Walla Walla people are

The Walla Walla are a Native people of the Columbia Plateau, with ancestral communities in what is now southeastern Washington and northeastern Oregon. Their lives have long been tied to the Columbia River and nearby waterways. Today the Walla Walla are one of the three peoples united in the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation, commonly called CTUIR, alongside the Cayuse and Umatilla. Each people retains its own heritage. [1, 19]

Walúulapam is a name used in CTUIR scholarship for the Walla Walla people. The tribal Umatilla dictionary also records Walawalałáma for Walla Walla people and Walawalałaamí sɨ́nwit for their language. These forms reflect different linguistic contexts and spelling conventions. [2, 12]

The CTUIR traces its peoples' presence in the Columbia River region back more than 10,000 years. Their history is rooted in oral traditions, ancestral places and continuing ties to the land. The modern confederated government grew from later treaty and constitutional arrangements. [1, 18]
Homeland and language

Walla Walla communities lived around Wallula and the meeting places of the Columbia, Walla Walla, Snake and Yakima rivers. Rivers linked villages, fisheries and trade routes. The Blue Mountains supplied other seasonal resources. The valley also carries an Indigenous place name meaning the place of the balsamroot sunflower, connecting geography with a useful native plant. [4, 9]

Walla Walla belongs to Sahaptin. The CTUIR Language Program describes it as a northeastern Sahaptin dialect, while Umatilla is a southern dialect. The original Cayuse language was different. The Weyíiletpuu variety taught today is a Nez Perce dialect used by Cayuse people. These language histories help explain why the three peoples should be studied as related communities with distinct identities. [3]

The tribal language program records speakers, protects older language materials and teaches learners of different ages. This work preserves place names, family knowledge and ways of describing relationships with the land. Language renewal is an active part of community life. [3]
Seasonal foods and daily work

Families followed a seasonal round, returning to known places as foods became available. They moved between river valleys and the mountains rather than depending on one crop or one settlement for everything. Drying fish, meat, roots and berries helped provide food through winter. [5]

blocks.text: Homes and family life

Tule plants supplied mats for shelters. Families placed these mats over pole frames to make longhouses and other lodges. When moving camp, they could carry the mats and use poles at another location. These homes suited a life organized around seasonal travel. [4]

Extended families worked together to obtain food and prepare supplies. Elders taught children skills and family history. Bands had their own headmen, whose influence depended on persuasion and the support of their people. Leadership was spread among communities rather than resting permanently in one ruler over every Walla Walla band. [4]

Lewis recorded fifteen large mat lodges at the village he visited on April 27, 1806. His entry also describes people supplying firewood and food to the expedition. This is a useful contemporary glimpse of a particular community, although it represents an outsider's brief visit. [6]
Trade and horses

Horses expanded travel, carrying capacity and contact with other peoples. Walla Walla families could move supplies overland more easily while keeping their close connection with rivers. The CTUIR's ethnographic study describes horse travel as an addition to a continuing river-based way of life. [12]

Trade involved social duties as well as goods. The leader whom Lewis and Clark called Yelleppit may have been identified by a Sahaptin term for a trading friend. Such relationships joined communities through gifts, hospitality and repeated exchanges. The familiar spelling in expedition records may therefore record a relationship rather than his personal name. [8]

In 1806 Yelleppit offered Clark a white horse. Clark, unable to spare the requested kettle, gave him a sword and other goods. The exchange shows how Walla Walla leaders pursued useful relationships with newcomers through established practices of giving and negotiation. [8]
Belief ceremony and responsibility

Tamánwit refers to traditional law and a way of life rooted in the Creator's ordering of the world. In CTUIR teachings, foods sustain people and people have a duty to care for the land and the living things that feed them. This relationship links spiritual responsibility with practical actions such as harvesting and caring for rivers. [12]

Some tribal members continue Washat, also called Seven Drums. Community worship includes singing, drumming and dancing. Traditional food gathering continues as well. These practices connect living families with earlier generations, while individual members have their own religious lives. [1]

First Foods are central to this relationship. A peer reviewed study by Eric Quaempts and colleagues explains how reciprocity, the duty to care for the beings that sustain people, guides CTUIR environmental management. Protecting foods requires attention to the wider ecosystems that allow them to return. [21]
Clothing and material arts

Historical Walla Walla objects show skilled work with hides, beads and other materials. A Smithsonian pouch dated to about the 1840s combines buffalo hide, sinew and large glass pony beads. Its block patterns show how makers used the size and shape of the beads in their designs. The object offers evidence of artistic choices and the movement of materials across regions. [10]

A Walla Walla dress dated to about 1860 to 1880 combines deerskin, glass beads, cowrie shells and sinew. It belongs to a deer-tail dress tradition shared by women in the eastern Plateau and northern Plains. Such objects show cultural exchange and individual workmanship. They document clothing from particular historical periods rather than a single outfit worn by every Walla Walla person. [11]
Encounters with explorers traders and missionaries

Lewis and Clark met Yelleppit in October 1805 and again during their return in April 1806. Walla Walla hosts supplied food, assistance and route information. Their knowledge of an overland trail helped the expedition shorten its journey toward Nez Perce country. The explorers depended on people who already understood the region. [7]

In his April 27 journal, Lewis described a leader who brought wood and roasted fish himself and encouraged others to help. The entry documents hospitality and leadership through example. It also reflects the expedition's immediate needs and its author's assumptions, so it should be read alongside tribal accounts. [6]

In 1818 the North West Company established Fort Nez Perce near the mouth of the Walla Walla River. It later became known as Fort Walla Walla. This was a fur-trade post near Wallula, distinct from the later United States military fort associated with today's city. Walla Walla headman Tamatapam helped develop trade with the Hudson's Bay Company. [8, 9]

The Whitman mission began in 1836 on Cayuse land with the permission of a Cayuse headman. Rising settlement and new diseases then placed severe pressure on Native communities. In 1847 a group of Cayuse attacked the mission during a crisis marked by a devastating measles outbreak. The mission's story belongs to the region's shared history, but the Walla Walla and Cayuse remain distinct peoples. [9, 24]
The Walla Walla treaty of 1855

United States officials Isaac Stevens and Joel Palmer sought treaties that would open Native lands to settlers and place tribal communities on reservations. Tribal leaders attended the Walla Walla council to protect their people and defend their relationship with the land. Their arguments drew on religious duties and the right to remain in their homeland. [13]

On June 9, 1855, Walla Walla, Cayuse and Umatilla delegates signed a treaty with the United States. The agreement ceded roughly 6.4 million acres and reserved a homeland in northeastern Oregon. The council involved other peoples too, who made separate treaties. The Walla Walla agreement should be distinguished from the Yakama and Nez Perce treaties negotiated at the same council. [13]

Article I reserved fishing within the reservation and at usual and accustomed stations outside it. It also protected hunting, gathering roots and berries and grazing stock on unclaimed lands under the treaty's terms. Other articles promised payments, buildings and services. The agreement treated the three peoples as one nation for treaty purposes. [14]

The Senate ratified the treaty on March 8, 1859. President James Buchanan proclaimed it on April 11, 1859. Signing in 1855 and ratification in 1859 were separate steps, and conflict had already erupted before ratification. [14, 15]
Peopeomoxmox and the fighting of 1855

Peopeomoxmox, also spelled Peo-Peo-Mox-Mox, was a prominent Walla Walla leader and treaty participant. In December 1855 he approached Oregon volunteer troops under a flag of truce and was held as a hostage. Fighting began on December 7 in the Walla Walla Valley, near Frenchtown, and continued for several days. [15]

On the first day of battle the volunteers killed Peopeomoxmox while he was in their custody. Accounts differ about the immediate struggle, but his captivity and death are established. The campaign scattered families and damaged their livestock-based wealth. It was part of a wider period of warfare across the Columbia Plateau, with lasting consequences for the ability of Native communities to remain in their homelands. [15]
Reservation life and allotment

Reservation life restricted older patterns of travel and access to resources. Walla Walla families joined Cayuse, Umatilla and other relatives in the reservation community. People continued harvesting foods while also adapting to farming, ranching and paid work. These changes involved both decisions made by families and pressures imposed by government policy. [16]

Allotment divided collectively held reservation land into individual parcels. Officials then opened land classified as surplus to non-Native acquisition. At Umatilla, the Slater Act of 1885 preceded the better-known General Allotment Act of 1887. Further legislation in 1888 reduced reservation lands. This process weakened the shared land base and made cultural and economic life more difficult. [16]
Schooling and cultural pressure

Federal education policy often aimed to replace Native languages and practices with English and Euro-American customs. A boarding school operated on the Umatilla Reservation, and off-reservation schools formed part of the wider system. Many children were separated from their families, and schooling could interrupt learning from parents and elders. [17]

The history of Native education also includes families seeking useful training and later efforts to reshape schools. Present tribal language teaching grows within this longer struggle over who controls education and what knowledge children receive. The harmful aims of early assimilation policy should be distinguished from the goals of contemporary Native education. [17, 3]
Constitutional government and community life

The confederated tribes ratified a constitution on November 4, 1949, by 113 votes to 104. Federal approval followed on December 7. The text declared that adopting the constitution would surrender no tribal rights and specified that it was not adopted under the Indian Reorganization Act. The document records the community's effort to strengthen self-government on its own terms. [18]

Today the CTUIR has a General Council of adult tribal members and an elected nine-member Board of Trustees. Its government works on education, health, natural resources and other community affairs. Walla Walla people participate in this shared political nation while maintaining family and cultural identities. Modern membership totals reported for CTUIR cover all three peoples together. [19]
Celilo Falls and the changing river

Celilo Falls was a major intertribal fishing and trading place on the Columbia River. Its significance extended beyond the communities living immediately beside it. Treaties preserved fishing rights, but commercial fishing, development and barriers to access placed pressure on Native fisheries. [20]

On March 10, 1957, the reservoir behind The Dalles Dam submerged the falls and part of Celilo Village. The loss removed fishing platforms and transformed a center of work and social life. Federal compensation for lost fishing sites did not extinguish tribal fishing rights. The event helps explain why the history of the Walla Walla and related river peoples includes the history of dams and river management. [20]
Cultural renewal and river restoration

Tamástslikt Cultural Institute opened to the public on August 1, 1998. It tells Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla history from tribal perspectives through exhibits and public programs. Its exhibits explain tribal experiences of western expansion and connect that history with community life today. [23]

The CTUIR Fisheries Habitat Program works with landowners, agencies and other partners to restore river conditions across traditional harvesting areas. Its approach includes floodplains, channels, streamside vegetation and the movement of water and fish. The purpose is to sustain aquatic First Foods and opportunities to harvest them. [22]

The First Foods approach connects these projects with older duties of care. Quaempts and colleagues explain that reciprocity can organize scientific planning and management decisions. In this setting, cultural continuity depends partly on whether rivers and surrounding lands can continue supporting the foods on which community life rests. [21]
