blocks.text: Tillamook History Culture and Timeline
Native communities of the northern Oregon Coast

The Tillamook are Indigenous people of the Oregon Coast whose ancestral language belongs to the Salishan language family. Their history includes independent coastal villages, skilled use of rivers and the ocean, severe losses from introduced diseases and continued community life after settlers took their lands. Tillamook heritage continues through descendants in several communities, including the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians, the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde and the Clatsop-Nehalem Confederated Tribes. [1–3]

This study explains their homelands, daily life and oral traditions, then follows the changes brought by foreign ships, American settlement and federal Indian policy. Numbered citations connect the text and timeline to the sources at the end.
Homelands and community identities

Tillamook communities lived along coastal rivers, bays and estuaries south of the lower Columbia River. Their settlements included the Nehalem and Tillamook Bay areas, Netarts and Nestucca, with related Tillamook-speaking communities farther south around Salmon River and Siletz. These waterways provided food and routes between the shore, forest and nearby mountains. An estuary is the place where a river meets the sea. [2–4]

The word Tillamook comes from Chinook usage for the people of Nekelim, or Nehalem. It became a broad name for related communities. Local people also identified themselves through particular villages and rivers. These identities did not always fit the fixed tribal divisions that government officials and later writers used. The Siletz Tribe identifies Nehalem, Nestucca, Salmon River and Siletz among the more specific affiliations covered by the general Tillamook name. [1–2]

Language and political identity need to be kept distinct. Tillamook was Salishan, while neighboring Clatsop people originally spoke a Chinookan language. Marriage, shared places and trade closely connected them. Archaeological evidence shows a long history of coastal occupation, but the age of a site does not by itself prove that its earliest residents used a particular modern tribal name or language. [3, 10]
Food homes and practical knowledge

Cedar plank houses provided permanent village homes. Families relied on salmon, lampreys, shellfish and other foods from the water, along with berries, camas and hunted animals such as deer and elk. Their economy drew on several environments rather than a single food supply. [4]

Coastal life followed seasonal opportunities. People moved between established settlements and places where particular foods could be gathered or caught. Nets, traps and weirs helped harvest fish. A weir is a barrier that guides fish toward an opening or trap. Processing and storing food helped households prepare for seasons when fresh supplies were harder to obtain. These practices belonged to a wider coastal economy, with local differences in technique and resources. [5]

Canoes carried people and goods along rivers, across bays and into coastal waters. Tillamook canoe workmanship impressed Lewis and Clark. Basket making was also a major skill. Together, watercraft and containers made it possible to gather, transport and exchange food efficiently. These were practical technologies that required detailed knowledge of wood, plant fibers and local water conditions. [8]
Family leadership and social rank

The village was an important political unit. The Siletz Tribe describes the region’s headmen as organizers and mediators who helped settle disputes and arrange work. Their authority was generally different from that of a European king. Family relationships also connected people across village boundaries, helping them maintain ties through marriage and exchange. [2–3]

Coastal societies had differences in wealth and inherited standing. Slavery existed among the Tillamook, although a regional history describes it as less common than among neighboring Chinook and Clatsop communities. Captives could be bought, sold or inherited. This part of social life belongs in a full account alongside cooperation, artistic work and family obligations. [5]
Basketry and cultural change

Tillamook basketry continued as life changed under American settlement. Anthropologist Ailsa Elizabeth Crawford studied the Adams Collection at the Tillamook County Pioneer Museum. Its 29 baskets, probably made between 1880 and 1940, were mostly small and made with raffia in commercial colors. They were documented as the work of Tillamook women, yet collectors and researchers had often overlooked them because their appearance did not match expectations of traditional Native art. [6]

The collection shows why cultural change requires careful study. New materials do not automatically make an object less connected to the people who made it. Crawford compared these baskets with earlier examples, examining materials, stitches, shapes and decorative techniques. Her research provides a way to study continued craftsmanship as well as change. [6]
Language stories and spiritual life

Tillamook oral traditions connect people, powerful beings and familiar places. In a story published by Franz Boas in 1898, a man goes salmon fishing on Slab Creek and encounters the Thunderer. The setting brings spiritual power into a landscape where people worked and obtained food. Boas collected the traditions at Siletz in 1890. His publication preserves valuable evidence, but its English wording and interpretation also reflect an outside recorder. [1]

Clara Pearson was a central source of Nehalem Tillamook knowledge in the twentieth century. Elizabeth Derr Jacobs worked with her in 1933 on accounts of community life, dreams and healing practices, then returned in 1934 to record stories. Pearson’s direction helped shape the interviews. Her narratives appeared in Nehalem Tillamook Tales in 1959, while The Nehalem Tillamook An Ethnography was published in 2003. These works depend on Pearson’s knowledge and skill as a storyteller. [7]

Such records are especially valuable for studying language and beliefs after decades of disruption. They also have limits. One person’s recollections cannot represent every village or every period. Descriptions of older customs should therefore be read in relation to the speaker, the place and the circumstances in which the record was made. [1, 7]
Ships trade and introduced disease

In August 1788, Captain Robert Gray’s Lady Washington visited Tillamook Bay. A violent encounter followed, and a member of Gray’s party, Marcos Lopez, was killed. Gray’s name for the harbor reflected the visiting crew’s view of that event. The episode illustrates how early maritime contact could combine efforts to obtain supplies with conflict. [8]

In January 1806, William Clark traveled south from Fort Clatsop toward a whale stranded near present-day Cannon Beach. Tillamook people had already processed much of it. Clark wanted meat, blubber and oil, but found that the traders had little interest in many of his goods. They had their own plans for exchange, including obtaining wapato roots through regional trade. [9]

Historian James Ronda explains that the explorers sometimes misunderstood coastal identities. Tillamook speakers used Chinook trade language with outsiders, which helped obscure their different language background. The journals are useful firsthand evidence, but they do not always classify communities accurately. [10]

Introduced diseases killed many Tillamook people. Epidemics in the 1830s were especially damaging. These losses weakened households and communities before large numbers of American settlers arrived. Early population reports used different boundaries and methods, so they should be treated as estimates rather than a consistent census. [4, 20]
Treaties reservations and land loss

In August 1851, federal officials negotiated the Tansy Point treaties near the Columbia River’s mouth. The participants included Nehalem and other Tillamook representatives. The agreements were never ratified by the United States. The promised arrangements therefore did not provide the protection that Native participants expected as settlement advanced. [11, 20]

A contemporary newspaper account, preserved with Oregon Indian Affairs correspondence, described the negotiations as completed land cessions. That wording shows how quickly American reports presented Native territory as available. It must be read alongside the later legal fact that the treaties were not ratified. The report records an American claim about acquisition, not proof that every promised term became binding or was carried out. [20]

On November 9, 1855, President Franklin Pierce established the Coast Reservation by executive order. It covered more than a million acres in western Oregon. Subsequent government actions repeatedly reduced it. The Grand Ronde and Siletz agencies administered communities brought together from many different peoples, and Grand Ronde became a separate reservation in 1857. [12]

Tillamook families experienced this process in different ways. Some became part of the reservation communities. David Lewis documents members of the Nehalem, Nestucca, Salmon River and Tillamook communities joining Grand Ronde between the 1860s and 1890s. Others continued living on the coast. It would be inaccurate to give every Tillamook family the same removal date or destination. [13–15]
Coastal communities that continued

At Hobsonville on Tillamook Bay, Chief Illga and other displaced families formed a community near the growing lumber and salmon-packing settlement. By the 1870s, it offered a place for Tillamook and some Clatsop families to regroup. In 1890, Illga arranged to purchase the village site. Residents maintained Tillamook language, stories and a hereditary chieftainship, and later worked with researchers recording their knowledge. [14]

Seaside’s Indian Place was another center of continued coastal life. Clatsop and Nehalem-Tillamook families gathered there after losing access to other homes. Chiefs Kotata and Dunkle helped lead the community. In 1879, Tsin-is-tum, also known as Jennie Michel, and her husband Michel Martineau purchased the village property. Their land and nearby Native holdings became a reserve created through private ownership. [15]

These communities depended on families who secured places to live and kept relationships active despite displacement. Their history explains how language and oral knowledge continued outside federally administered reservations. [14–15]
Termination restoration and community life today

The Western Oregon Indian Termination Act of 1954 ended federal relationships with numerous western Oregon tribal communities through a process implemented during the following years. Termination threatened landholding, services and organized political life. Family networks continued, and Native leaders worked to rebuild federal relationships. [13, 16]

The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians regained federal recognition on November 18, 1977. Grand Ronde regained recognition on November 22, 1983. These restorations concerned confederations with many ancestral peoples, including Tillamook descendants. They did not create a single new government representing every person of Tillamook ancestry. [2–3, 16–17]

Cultural work remains part of tribal community life. The Siletz cultural program documents history, protects ancestral sites and collections, teaches arts and holds gatherings for families. Its language instruction emphasizes Siletz Athabaskan. That language belongs to a different family from ancestral Tillamook Salishan, so the two should not be confused. [1, 18]

On May 5, 2020, North Coast Land Conservancy transferred 18.6 acres at Neawanna Point in Seaside to the Clatsop-Nehalem Confederated Tribes. The land includes saltmarsh and Sitka spruce forest at the Necanicum Estuary. This return of land to a living descendant community gives a recent example of continued connections to ancestral places. [19]
People to know
Chief Kilchis was a leading Tillamook Bay figure during the period when American settlers entered the area. [14]
Chief Illga helped establish Hobsonville as a home for displaced families and arranged the village land purchase. [14]
Kóshtawah, also known as Maggie Adams, married Illga and became a matriarch of the Hobsonville community. Her family connections linked Clatsop and Tillamook histories. [21]
Clara Pearson preserved Nehalem Tillamook stories and detailed knowledge of community life through her work with Elizabeth Derr Jacobs. [7]
Tsin-is-tum, or Jennie Michel, helped sustain Seaside’s Indian Place through landownership and support for other Native families. [15]

blocks.text: Squamish History Culture and Timeline
The Sḵwx̱wú7mesh people of British Columbia

Squamish history joins an ancient homeland with continuing efforts to protect community life. Salmon, cedar, language and family relationships connect cultural practice with struggles over land and government. The study below follows that history from early village life through colonial disruption, the union of 1923 and present cultural renewal. Numbered references lead to the sources at the end. [1, 5, 16]
Who the Squamish are

The Squamish, or Sḵwx̱wú7mesh, are an Indigenous Coast Salish people of southwestern British Columbia, Canada. Their present government is called Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw, the Squamish Nation. Many members live on Vancouver’s North Shore and along the Squamish River. Their history reaches back thousands of years before the united government took shape in 1923. [1, 3]

Coast Salish refers to a broad group of related peoples and languages. It does not mean that all those peoples share one government or the same traditions. Squamish history is closely tied to neighbouring communities, including the Lil’wat, Musqueam and Tsleil-Waututh, while remaining a distinct history. [4, 23]
Homeland and ancient history

The Nation describes a traditional territory of 6,732 square kilometres. It includes Howe Sound and its islands, the Squamish Valley, Burrard Inlet and mountain watersheds reaching toward Whistler. These places connect salt water, river valleys, forests and high country. The broad homeland is much larger than the reserve lands later recognized by colonial governments. [2]

The Nation cites archaeological evidence dating back about 8,600 years. This supports a deep history of human presence. It should not be treated as a precise date when the people first became Squamish. Oral traditions describe ancestral beginnings and continuing relationships with particular places through a different form of historical knowledge. [1, 3]

Squamish archaeologist Rudy Reimer’s research also shows that mountain country was an active part of the homeland. People used high areas for resources and travelled through landscapes that outsiders sometimes assumed were too harsh for regular use. Reimer connects archaeological evidence with oral traditions and place names. His work helps explain why Squamish history cannot be told only from the shoreline. [4]
Homes families and seasonal life

Families lived in large cedar plank longhouses that could hold several related households. People moved among village sites and residences according to the season. These moves followed established relationships and harvesting patterns. A village temporarily used by fewer people was still part of an inhabited homeland. Today longhouses continue to serve as places for ceremony. [3, 5]

The word úxwumixw can refer to a village, community, people or nation. The Nation’s explanation joins the physical place with the people who belong to it. Family upbringing also carries a strong moral meaning. Children learn how to conduct themselves and care for others through the guidance of relatives and community members. [7]
Food resources and travel

Salmon has long been a major food. Smoking and wind drying allowed fish to be stored for later use. Canning became another method in more recent times. Preserving a harvest mattered because families needed food beyond the brief period when a particular resource was plentiful. [5]

The wider food economy reached beyond salmon. Coastal people gathered shellfish and other shoreline foods, while mountain use included hunting and gathering. Reimer describes mountain goat hunting and the value of high country plants that ripened later than plants at lower elevations. Different environments extended the places and seasons in which food could be obtained. [4, 12]

Cedar supplied material for ocean-going dugout canoes, fishing weirs, bark weaving and root baskets. A weir is a barrier that guides or traps fish. These uses show how one tree supported travel, food gathering and skilled craft. Canoes linked households and villages across waterways that remain central to Squamish identity. [5]
Language and teaching

Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Sníchim, the Squamish language, belongs to the Salishan language family. It is a distinct language rather than a form of English or one common language spoken by every Coast Salish people. Learning it preserves ways of describing social relationships and the homeland. [8]

The Nation identifies respect, advice and good upbringing among its guiding values. Snew̓íyelh refers to advice or teachings, while wanáxws concerns treating someone with respect. These ideas help explain how education takes place in everyday family life as well as in formal classes. A person’s conduct matters alongside the knowledge that person possesses. [7]

Place names also hold knowledge. The Nation’s land account connects names with oral traditions and with places such as villages, hunting camps, cedar gathering areas and cemeteries. Losing a name can therefore weaken access to a story or relationship associated with the place. Language renewal helps restore those connections. [2, 8]
Beliefs ceremony and leadership

Squamish traditions connect ancestors, powerful beings and particular places. In the flood account shared by the Nation, ancestors secured their canoes to Nch’ḵay̓, Mount Garibaldi, and survived. The account belongs to Squamish oral tradition and expresses a relationship with the mountain. Archaeological dating alone cannot assign it a single calendar date. [5]

The Nation’s Heritage Policy connects inherited rights and responsibilities with language, ceremony, ancestral places and knowledge passed to future generations. Heritage includes living relationships and duties. Protecting a place therefore involves more than keeping old objects intact. [6]

The title siy̓ám̓ can identify an honoured or highly respected person. The Cultural Centre discusses hereditary chieftainship alongside the elected leadership of the modern Nation. These roles have different histories and should not be reduced to one timeless system of government. Family ties, knowledge and public responsibilities all matter in understanding leadership. [7, 25]

Potlatches, within the wider Northwest Coast setting, bring people together to witness events such as names, marriages, changes in leadership and claims to rights. Gifts help recognize the witnesses and their obligation to remember. The details differ among peoples and families. The social, political and spiritual functions explain why attempts to suppress such gatherings had effects far beyond entertainment or feasting. [11]
Weaving carving and clothing

Blankets provided warmth and could carry ceremonial meaning. The Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre describes their use in weddings, namings, coming of age events and funerals. A person may be wrapped in a blanket as an honour. The meaning depends on the ceremony and on how the blanket is presented. [9]

The Cultural Centre links some of its wool weaving designs and techniques with blankets worn by Squamish chiefs who travelled to England in 1906 to raise land concerns. Clothing could express identity and standing during political action. Its canoe apprenticeship program also teaches forms that had not been built locally for several generations. [10]

Carving remains a living art. During the 2023 centennial, master carver Xwalacktun worked on a commemorative house post while mentoring Brandon Hall. The project joined public memory with direct teaching. It is an example of cultural knowledge being carried forward through skilled work and personal relationships. [25]
European encounters disease and missions

In June 1792, George Vancouver’s expedition encountered Squamish people in the Burrard Inlet area. This is a documented European encounter within an already occupied homeland. It does not mark the beginning of local history or mean that Squamish communities had previously lived without trade and contact with their neighbours. [12]

Epidemics damaged Indigenous communities throughout the region. Historian Robert Boyd’s research, summarized by HistoryLink, places a major Northwest Coast smallpox epidemic in the 1770s. An account told by a Squamish elder to Charles Hill-Tout in the 1890s recalled severe illness and loss. That later recollection offers evidence of remembered devastation, though it cannot by itself establish an exact local death count or date. Regional estimates should not be presented as exact Squamish population figures. [13]

Catholic missionary activity became another force in community life. MONOVA records a Catholic mass at Eslha7an in 1860 and the construction of St Paul’s Church there in 1868. Mission activity introduced new institutions and beliefs. Its history needs to be distinguished from the later residential school, even though church and school histories became closely connected. [12, 19]
Reserves and the changing economy

Between 1876 and 1888, reserves were surveyed and allotted at Squamish villages and traditional food gathering places. The Nation records 26 reserves in this process. Authorities claimed the rest as Crown land. Reserve boundaries narrowed the land base recognized by colonial government without erasing Squamish connections to the wider territory. [3]

As nearby cities and industry grew, reserve land was leased, sold or taken. This placed pressure on homes and access to resources. These changes also affected relationships within Squamish society, because separate government-recognized bands did not always match wider family networks and shared interests. [3, 16]

Squamish people also worked in the industrial economy. Historian Fred Burrill’s discussion of Andrew Parnaby’s waterfront research shows that paid dock work and union organizing became important parts of Squamish community life. Industrial employment could help support families and resistance to colonial control. [14]

Changes in hiring and demands for a more fixed working schedule later disadvantaged workers who combined dock labour with other activities. This history complicates a simple story in which Indigenous people remained outside the modern economy. Squamish workers helped build that economy while facing pressures that limited their choices within it. [14]
The destruction of Senakw in 1913

Sen̓áḵw stood on the south shore of False Creek in present day Vancouver. In 1913, Squamish families were forced from the village. The homes were burned and the land was divided for settler use. This was the loss of an inhabited community within a rapidly growing city. [24]

Mayana C Slobodian’s study of contemporary newspapers and the later inquiry shows that the transaction was controversial at the time. Accounts described threats that people would receive nothing if they refused the offered payment. The sale and removal were therefore not simply accepted by everyone as ordinary land business. [15]

Slobodian argues that much of the public scandal focused on the conduct of officials and Canada’s reputation for fairness. Concern over those issues often failed to produce justice for the displaced families. This is a historical interpretation drawn from the newspaper record. It helps explain how public criticism can coexist with continued land loss. [15]
Political leadership and the union of 1923

In 1906, Squamish chiefs travelled to England to bring land concerns before King Edward VII. Such actions show that Squamish leaders actively challenged the treatment of their people rather than simply accepting government decisions. Political advocacy continued through later petitions and organizing. [10]

Andy Paull worked with Chief Harry and other leaders on the movement toward amalgamation, meaning the union of separate bands under one administration. Land sales had produced unequal payments: benefits could go only to members of the band whose reserve was involved, despite wider family connections. Pooling property and funds offered a way to address this division. [16]

The Prayer of Amalgamation was approved on January 26, 1923. On July 23, sixteen bands with a combined population of 412 united as the Squamish Nation. The union created a common administration and consolidated interests held in trust. It was a major political turning point within a much older people’s history. [16]

Paull’s wider work also reached beyond local administration. Brendan F R Edwards shows how he used letters, public argument and newspapers to support Indigenous rights. He was involved in organizations including the Allied Tribes of British Columbia and the North American Indian Brotherhood. His use of English writing became a tool for challenging outsiders’ claims about Indigenous people. [17]
Residential schools and restrictions on culture

St Paul’s Residential School in North Vancouver operated from 1899 to 1959. The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation identifies it as a Catholic institution. Its history forms part of the residential school system, which sought to change Indigenous children’s identities and separate education from the authority of their families. [19, 27]

The federal government also restricted cultural practices through the Indian Act. The 1884 amendment banning potlatches attacked institutions through which communities passed on names, rights and obligations. The prohibition remained until the 1951 revision. Many communities continued ceremonies despite the law. This was a regional policy affecting Coast Salish and other Northwest Coast peoples, not a law directed only at the Squamish. [11]

Today the Squamish-led Yúusnew̓as project records residential school experiences and conducts archival and land-based research. It works with Musqueam and Tsleil-Waututh communities and combines investigation with support for survivors and families. Knowledge keepers help guide the work. The project makes community testimony and care central to the recovery of this history. [20]
Preserving memory and renewing language

Chief August Jack Khahtsahlano helped preserve detailed knowledge of Squamish life. Conversations recorded by Vancouver archivist J S Matthews between 1932 and 1954 were published in 1955. They include family history and accounts of local events. Because Matthews selected and transcribed the material, readers should distinguish Khahtsahlano’s testimony from the archivist’s comments and framing. [18]

Language renewal has required deliberate work. In 2016, Kwi Awt Stelmexw partnered with Simon Fraser University to begin a full-time adult immersion program. A 2017 university report described the effort to create new fluent speakers. Another SFU account reported fifteen new speakers after the first year. These are dated reports about a program, rather than a current census of all speakers. [21, 22]

The Nation’s Language and Cultural Affairs department supports language, heritage and archives with guidance from Elders, speakers and community partners. Its work serves members both on and off reserve. This matters because belonging and cultural learning continue across different places of residence. [26]
Cooperation land recovery and the present

The Squamish and Lil’wat Nations signed a cooperation protocol in 2001. Their Cultural Centre opened in Whistler in July 2008. Its architecture draws on Squamish longhouses and Lil’wat pit houses. The partnership gives both Nations a place to teach while showing that shared interests do not erase their distinct cultures. [23]

The Nation’s Sacred Land Use Plan grew out of community work begun in 2000, including feasts, interviews and workshops with Elders and youth. It connects decisions about land with cultural responsibilities and future generations. Stewardship is therefore also a matter of community planning and political authority. [2, 6]

After decades of advocacy, part of Sen̓áḵw returned to Squamish control in the early 2000s. The Nation’s project account dates the return of 10.48 acres to 2003. Members approved redevelopment in 2019. The housing project links a return to ancestral land with income and homes. Construction plans and projected benefits describe intended outcomes, rather than proof that every promised result has already occurred. [24]

The 2023 centennial marked one hundred years of united government. Exhibitions and new artistic work connected that anniversary with family histories and the continuing homeland. Squamish history remains a story of people governing, teaching and making decisions in the present, as well as remembering earlier generations. [25]

blocks.text: Jumano History Culture and Timeline
West Texas the Southern Plains and the Rio Grande borderlands
Who the Jumano were

The Jumano were Indigenous people associated with West Texas, the Southern Plains, eastern New Mexico and northern Mexico. Their best documented role was as bison hunters, traders and diplomats who connected communities across this large region. Their history shows how Native peoples built and maintained exchange networks long before modern state and national borders. [6]

The name needs care. Spanish writers used Jumano and related spellings for people in widely separated places, including mobile hunting groups and Pueblo communities. Scholars disagree about how closely all these groups were related. It is useful to distinguish the mobile traders from their village partners while recognizing that some may have shared language, relatives or a wider identity. [5, 6]
Homelands and early roots

A key meeting place was La Junta de los Ríos, where the Río Conchos joins the Rio Grande near present Presidio, Texas and Ojinaga, Chihuahua. Its river valleys supported farms within the surrounding desert. The location helped connect farming villages with mobile hunters and traders. Jumano journeys linked La Junta with the Southern Plains and reached Caddo communities in East Texas. [18]

By about 1200 CE, and possibly earlier, farming villages existed at La Junta. Archaeologists have found houses, pottery and imported objects that connect these settlements with the wider Southwest, including the Casas Grandes or Paquimé exchange network. These discoveries describe the region’s earlier history. They do not establish that every early village was occupied by people who later called themselves Jumano. [3]

Scholars have proposed both migration from the Jornada Mogollon region farther northwest and local adoption of farming and village life. The evidence does not settle the issue. A pottery style can show contact or trade without proving that the people who used it belonged to the same ethnic group as its makers. [3, 4]
Names and language

Colonial names were often inconsistent. Spanish officials could apply an outside nickname to people who had different names for themselves. At La Junta, for example, the label Patarabueye grouped together village populations that had more specific names and spoke different languages. Treating every person at La Junta as Jumano hides this diversity. [7]

The language of the mobile Jumano is not securely classified. There is no substantial surviving language record that resolves the question. Nancy Parrott Hickerson argued for a Tanoan connection with eastern Pueblo peoples. Earlier scholars proposed other affiliations or treated Jumano as a broad label rather than one people. The Tanoan view is an important scholarly argument, but it should be presented as an interpretation rather than a proven identification. [5]
Food homes and material culture

Mobile Jumano depended heavily on bison hunting. They exchanged meat and hides for crops from village partners. Clothing described in Spanish accounts included dressed animal skins, short garments and weather protection such as cloaks. Both men and women wore clothing, even when Europeans described them as naked by European standards. [1, 2]

Housing reflected different ways of living. Mobile hunters used hide tents. People staying in more lasting camps could build shelters of reeds or sticks, while associated Pueblo populations occupied masonry buildings. Jumano hunters used bows and arrows. Spanish observers noted strong bows reinforced with sinew, the tough tissue that connects muscle to bone. [1]

The La Junta villagers combined farming with gathering, fishing and hunting. Their fields supplied crops such as corn, beans and squash, while wild foods reduced dependence on a single harvest. These cultivators maintained relationships with mobile peoples, including Jumano visitors. A village community should not be assumed to represent the daily life of every Jumano hunting band. [7]

Spanish accounts also describe distinctive horizontal facial markings. These made some Jumano readily recognizable to outsiders. The markings may have involved tattooing, scarification, paint or a combination. The precise technique is uncertain. It is safer to describe the recorded appearance than to assign one method to every group. [1]
Trade and political relationships

Jumano traders exchanged products between hunting and farming communities and linked the Rio Grande region with peoples farther east, especially the Caddo. Seasonal journeys brought hunters toward the Plains and back toward village partners. After adopting horses, traders could move goods over greater distances. Spanish objects and horses reached eastern communities through these connections. [2]

This system required relationships as well as routes. The ability to arrange visits and speak for allies helped leaders bring otherwise separate communities into negotiations. Otermín’s August 1683 letter describes several Jumano captains asking for Spanish aid alongside their Julime neighbors. The record gives a picture of diplomacy involving multiple leaders and communities rather than evidence for a single government controlling every group called Jumano. [8]

Gran Quivira, also called Las Humanas, illustrates the Pueblo side of these connections. The National Park Service identifies its residents as eastern Tompiro/Jumano people and estimates a peak population of 1,500 to 3,000. Its location made it a place where Plains and Pueblo peoples could meet and trade. That site population is not an estimate for all Jumano people. [13]
Spanish contact and colonial pressure

In 1535, Cabeza de Vaca and his companions visited La Junta. His description of the People of the Cows is often connected with Jumano history. The exact identities of those he met remain uncertain. [10]

The Rodríguez–Chamuscado expedition passed through the area in 1581. The Espejo expedition of 1582–1583 supplied further descriptions and encountered Jumano guides near the Pecos on its return journey. These expeditions left useful observations, although the writers interpreted communities through Spanish names and interests. [10]

Relations with Spain involved both danger and opportunity. Slave raiding threatened Native communities, while European diseases and drought increased insecurity. Jumano leaders nevertheless sought missions and military alliances. Kenmotsu interprets these requests as efforts to gain protection and preserve access to land and trade. Religious interest and political need could exist together; the surviving records cannot reveal every person’s motives. [11]
Religion and the Lady in Blue tradition

Much of the written evidence about Jumano religion comes through Catholic missionaries, whose main concern was conversion. The Lady in Blue tradition became especially influential. María de Jesús de Ágreda, a nun who remained in Spain, reported spiritual visits to Indigenous people in the Southwest. Franciscan accounts linked her to Jumano requests for missionaries. [12]

Her reported appearances belong to the history of religious belief. They do not establish that she physically traveled to Texas or that a miracle occurred. The accounts also helped missionaries explain their work and seek support. The documented exchanges between Jumano leaders and Franciscans can be studied separately from the supernatural explanation attached to them. [12]

Accounts from La Junta describe gatherings with singing, clapping and dancing. These are valuable glimpses of local social life, but they are not a complete record of Jumano ceremonies. Nor should the practices of every La Junta community be assumed to have been identical. [10]
Juan Sabeata and the alliance of 1683

Juan Sabeata was an important Jumano spokesman in the late seventeenth century. On October 20, 1683, he gave testimony at El Paso seeking Spanish friendship, missionaries and assistance against Apache enemies. The University of Arizona’s archival description identifies testimony taken through an interpreter. Its references to many potential converts represent claims made during negotiations, not a reliable census of the Jumano population. [9]

Translated passages presented by Kenmotsu show Sabeata describing food, bison products and access to other peoples, including the Tejas or Caddo. He understood that these offers might interest Spanish authorities. His diplomacy linked his people’s security needs with Spanish hopes for converts, supplies and influence. [11]

The resulting expedition under Juan Domínguez de Mendoza and Franciscan Nicolás López left the El Paso area in December 1683. It traveled through La Junta and continued into Texas in 1684. It did not establish the lasting protective alliance Jumano leaders sought. Scholars also disagree about the expedition’s precise route and the location of its San Clemente camp. [17]
Dispersal and survival

The weakening of Jumano communities had several causes. Drought and food shortages damaged village life and hunting. Disease reduced populations. Slave raiding and colonial demands created further pressure, while conflict over hunting territory and trade access disrupted regional relationships. At Gran Quivira, the National Park Service attributes abandonment by 1672 to a combination of disease, drought, famine and Apache raiding. [4, 14]

Around the end of the seventeenth century, Jumano trading networks became harder to maintain. Some surviving groups later joined Apache communities. Others entered mixed settlements or moved into colonial communities farther south. A name becoming less common in official records does not prove that every person or family carrying that heritage died. [2, 4]

Modern community activity makes this distinction especially important. A Texas House resolution records the establishment of the Jumano Indian Nation of Texas council on May 22, 2016. The House honored the nation in May 2019. This was a commemorative resolution, not a grant of federal tribal recognition. [15]

Humanities Texas documented a September 2021 program in which Jumano Nation members planned to discuss history, culture and family connections with the public in Marfa. Such community work provides evidence of an active Jumano identity in modern West Texas. It also gives present-day descendants a voice in a history that older accounts often told only through colonial records. [16]
Timeline
Dates before Spanish contact describe the region’s archaeological history. Later entries distinguish recorded events from uncertain identifications.

blocks.text: Tittabawassee Ojibwe Communities
History Culture and Timeline

Tittabawassee is best understood as a local name connected with Native communities along Michigan's Tittabawassee River. The nineteenth-century treaty record places these communities within the wider Chippewa, or Ojibwe, world of the Saginaw Valley. The name should therefore be read in relation to local bands and villages, rather than assumed to identify a separate modern tribal nation. Their history belongs within the history of the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan, whose constituent bands are Saginaw, Swan Creek and Black River. [1, 2]

The river communities supported themselves through knowledge of the seasons, waterways and forests. U.S. treaties reduced their land base and threatened removal from Michigan. Later agreements established a homeland in Isabella County. Their descendants maintained community ties through land loss and the boarding school era, and continue cultural education and environmental work today. [10–13, 14–18]
Homeland and early history

The Tittabawassee country lies in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, around the river system associated with present-day Midland and the wider Saginaw Valley. The river appears in early treaties under spellings such as Tetabawasink and Tetabwasing. These changing spellings reflect the way English-language records represented Native place names. The 1819 treaty specifically identifies communities at the Little Forks and Black Bird's town. [2, 10]

Archaeological sites show a much longer Indigenous history than the surviving U.S. treaty record. A 1931 University of Michigan archaeological atlas, later supplied to the Environmental Protection Agency by tribal cultural staff, recorded six village sites within eight miles of present-day Midland. Such a compilation records evidence of settlement across time. It does not establish that all the sites were occupied together or belonged to one unchanged tribal group. [19]

Archaeologist James E. Fitting showed why the early Saginaw Valley should be understood as an area used by several peoples. Accounts of Henri Nouvel's winter journey in 1675–1676 describe travel through the Tittabawassee system and seasonal camps associated with Amikwa, Nipissing and other Native groups. Later records show a stronger Ojibwe presence in the valley during the eighteenth century. The regional history therefore includes movement, shared hunting areas and changing relationships among communities. [3]

This distinction matters when reading older accounts of battles between the Ojibwe and Sauk. Fitting questioned simple stories of one people occupying the whole valley and then being completely replaced. These accounts cannot establish a precise founding date for the river communities. [3]
Culture and daily life

The following practices come from Saginaw Chippewa cultural accounts and regional scholarship. They explain the wider Ojibwe and Anishinaabe setting of the river communities. Customs and teachings varied between families, communities and periods. [5–8]
Food and the seasons

Families planned their work around the availability of food. Fishing and hunting were central, while gathering and garden work also formed part of the wider Anishinaabe food system. Regional evidence describes warmer-season fishing, autumn deer hunting and smaller winter hunting groups. Seasonal movement allowed people to use different resources at different times. [3, 5]

Maple sugar making brought families together as winter gave way to spring. People collected sap, maintained fires and carefully processed it into syrup or sugar. Birchbark containers and carved wooden bowls required considerable preparation. The Ziibiwing Center explains that maple sugar provided food, energy and a trade item. It also describes sugaring as a time of reunion and celebration. Its account connects present-day sugaring on the Isabella Reservation with earlier generations. [5]
Homes and river travel

Birchbark was a major material in Anishinaabe life. People covered sapling lodge frames with large bark panels and made containers by joining bark with plant fibers. Birchbark canoes could carry people and goods through connected rivers and lakes, then be carried overland between waterways. These skills help explain how river communities could maintain contact across a large region. They also show why control of a riverbank alone cannot describe the full area used by a community. [6]
Language and family ties

The heritage language was Ojibwe, also called Anishinaabemowin. It belongs to the Central Algonquian language family. Ojibwe is spoken in several regional varieties, so a dictionary based on Minnesota and Wisconsin speech should not automatically be treated as a record of historical Tittabawassee pronunciation. Language carries place names, family knowledge and teachings, as well as everyday speech. [4]

Clan relationships linked people beyond their immediate households. The Ziibiwing Center describes clans associated with animals such as the bear, crane, loon and catfish. In its teachings, children traditionally belonged to their father's clan. Clan identity carried duties of care: members were expected to look after relatives and receive visiting members of the same clan. Clan symbols also appeared on treaties. These ties were broader than residence in a particular river village. [7]
Beliefs and practical knowledge

Spiritual teachings connected human responsibilities with animals, plants and the Creator. In the Ziibiwing account of Nenaboozhoo and the maple trees, easy access to syrup is changed so people must work for it and attend to their other responsibilities. The story teaches appreciation and effort. Its cultural meaning should be distinguished from a dated account of a specific historical event. [5]

Birchbark teachings similarly join practical knowledge with spiritual responsibilities. The Ziibiwing Center describes giving thanks when harvesting bark and caring for sacred scrolls through the Midewiwin Society. These public teachings describe parts of Anishinaabe religious life without implying that every family followed identical practices. [6]

Black ash basketry required identifying suitable trees, pounding the wood and preparing splints for weaving. Music included inherited songs as well as new forms. The tribe's cultural programs also explain the importance of cradleboards, plant knowledge and dance. Contemporary powwows draw on traditions from several Native peoples and should not be projected unchanged into the distant past. [8]
A Native account of the river communities

Andrew J. Blackbird, an Odawa writer and interpreter, provides a useful personal account in his 1887 history. While traveling south through Michigan in winter to seek support for Native citizenship, he and his companions ran short of food. Following the frozen Tittabawassee, they found one deserted camp and then another occupied by women and children while the men hunted. The residents fed the travelers. [9, chap. 7]

Blackbird was an Odawa visitor, so his account is not a complete description of a Tittabawassee community. It does, however, give direct evidence of winter camps, hospitality and travel along the river. His larger purpose was to explain Native efforts to secure their future and avoid removal. [9]
Treaties and the loss of local reserves
The Saginaw treaty of 1819

On September 24, 1819, U.S. commissioner Lewis Cass and Chippewa representatives signed the Treaty of Saginaw. It ceded a large territory while reserving several smaller tracts for Native use. Article 2 retained 6,000 acres at the Little Forks and another 6,000 acres at Black Bird's town on the Tittabawassee. These provisions are especially valuable evidence of local Native communities. [2, art. 2]

Article 5 also provided for hunting and maple sugar making on ceded land while it remained U.S. property. This was a conditional treaty provision. It did not guarantee that the entire ceded territory would remain permanently available for those activities. [2, art. 5]
The removal treaties of 1837

The January 14, 1837 treaty ceded numerous reserves retained in 1819, including both 6,000-acre Tittabawassee tracts. Article 6 called for the Saginaw Chippewa to leave Michigan once a suitable location could be obtained. The agreement also made removal expenses chargeable against the proceeds from their own lands. Its signatories included Ogima Keegido and other leaders representing the Saginaw bands. [10, arts. 1 and 6]

A second treaty, signed on December 20, 1837, specified a proposed home on the headwaters of the Osage River. It directed that fifty cents per acre from the earlier cession be retained for a new location and migration. These documents establish the government's removal plans. They should not be read as proof that every Saginaw Chippewa family was actually moved west. Later treaties provided a homeland within Michigan. [11, arts. 1–2; 12–13]
A homeland in Isabella County

The treaty of August 2, 1855 covered the Chippewa of Saginaw and the Swan Creek and Black River people remaining in Michigan. It withdrew unsold federal land in six adjoining Isabella County townships from public sale, along with a separate tract near Saginaw Bay. Eligible people could select individual parcels. The agreement promised money, tools, educational support and mills. It was signed in 1855 and ratified in 1856. [12]

These provisions offered a way to remain in Michigan, but tied assistance to permanent settlement and individual landholding. Article 6 also attempted to dissolve tribal organization except for carrying out the agreement. That clause expresses U.S. policy at the time. The continuing Saginaw Chippewa community and government demonstrate that Native political life endured. [12, art. 6; 1]

The October 18, 1864 treaty, ratified in 1866, reaffirmed land in Isabella County while relinquishing the earlier Saginaw Bay townships. It expanded categories of people eligible for land selections and directed federal officials to classify recipients by their supposed ability to manage property. Some received unrestricted titles; others needed federal consent to sell. These categories placed outside officials in a powerful position over Native families. [13, arts. 1–3]
Land loss and the boarding school era

A permanent reservation did not ensure secure family ownership. The Ziibiwing Center recounts delayed payments, hunger and illness after relocation. Families sometimes sold valuable timber land cheaply to obtain food, while dealings involving agents and lumber interests accelerated land loss. The center reports that only a small portion of the more than 1,500 nineteenth-century allotments remained in tribal hands by 1934. [14]

The Mount Pleasant Indian Industrial Boarding School operated from 1893 to 1934. It belonged to a wider system intended to assimilate Native children into the dominant society. Separating children from home and suppressing Native ways harmed the transmission of language and family knowledge. The Saginaw Chippewa later undertook research, remembrance and preservation at the site. In 2011, the tribe accepted former school property and began its Honoring, Healing and Remembering observance. [8, 15]
Continuing community and government

The Saginaw Chippewa reorganized under the Indian Reorganization Act in 1937. This was a change in governmental structure, not the beginning of the people themselves. The tribe's own historical account describes the long struggle to rebuild its land base and support community life. [1, 14]

Education under tribal direction became one part of that work. The Tribal Council established Saginaw Chippewa Tribal College in 1998 to expand access to higher education while sustaining cultural continuity. The Ziibiwing Center opened in 2004 as a place to preserve and share history, language and lifeways. These institutions allow the community to guide how its own history is taught. [16, 1]

On November 23, 2010, a federal court approved a negotiated settlement recognizing the entire Isabella Reservation as Indian Country. Agreements among the tribe, United States, Michigan and local governments addressed practical questions of jurisdiction. This settlement is a useful reminder that changes in ownership and government services did not simply erase the reservation. [17]

The connection to the river country also continues. In a November 20, 2012 letter to the EPA, the tribe sought protection of culturally significant sites and procedures for discoveries during cleanup along the Tittabawassee and Saginaw system. A natural resource damage settlement finalized in 2020 included funding for tribal acquisition and restoration of culturally valuable habitat near Saginaw Bay. Hunting, fishing and gathering remain part of the reason these wetlands matter. [18–19]

blocks.text: Alsea History Culture and Timeline

The Alsea are an Indigenous people of the central Oregon coast. Their history connects coastal villages, fishing places and oral traditions with the loss of land under United States rule. Alsea descendants remain part of the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians. This study follows their homeland, cultural life and history through the reservation era and into the present. [1, 4]
Homeland and identity

Alsea communities lived around the Alsea River estuary near present-day Waldport and along nearby parts of the coast, including Seal Rock, Yachats and Cape Perpetua. The Siletz Tribe explains that the name Alsea comes from alsíiya, a name neighboring peoples used for the Alsea and a name associated with the Alsea homeland. Ya’xaik was the Alsea village whose name survives in the modern name Yachats. [1, 2]

The coast offered connected food sources in rivers, estuaries, forests and the ocean. Trails also crossed the Coast Range toward the Willamette Valley, and people made seasonal gathering trips into the upper Alsea Valley. Alsea life therefore linked permanent villages with travel to places where particular foods and materials were available. [3, 15]

Alsea and neighboring Yaquina speech were closely connected and are often described as varieties of the same language. Older sources use Yakonan as a linguistic label. This should not erase local village identities or confuse Alsea with every other language spoken by the many peoples who later joined the Siletz confederation. [1, 4, 6]
Culture and daily life
Food and care for the land

Alsea families fished, hunted and gathered shellfish. Clams and mussels were important at Cape Perpetua. In the wider coastal economy, salmon and other fish were combined with gathered plant foods and hunted animals. Seasonal knowledge mattered: people needed to understand fish runs, tides and the places where useful plants grew. [2, 3]

People also shaped their surroundings. Research on Cape Perpetua describes Native burning that helped maintain open coastal prairies. After this burning ended, Sitka spruce expanded into formerly open ground. The landscape was thus partly the result of generations of human care and use. [2]
Villages homes and travel

Alsea life belonged to the central Oregon coast pattern of permanent villages and seasonal camps. Plank houses, often with floors or hearths below ground level, provided shelter. Across the coast, canoes and trails connected communities and gathering places. [3, 4]

The Siletz Tribe describes the older villages as largely self-governing. Headmen organized work and helped settle disputes. Their authority depended on community relationships and responsibilities. It is misleading to imagine all Alsea villages as a single centralized state ruled by one chief. [4]
Basketry clothing and adornment

Basketry was both skilled art and practical equipment. A 1981 Siletz tribal newsletter, drawing on historian Stephen Dow Beckham, describes basketry hats and burden baskets used by coastal women. It specifically records long hair among Alsea men and women and discusses shell and seed ornaments within the broader coastal tradition. Dentalium shells, which are slender marine shells, served as valued adornments. Some details in this account describe several coastal peoples together rather than Alsea people alone. [5]
Stories and spiritual knowledge

Alsea oral traditions connected people with animals, rivers and powerful beings. Stories recorded from Alsea speakers include S’uuku, a Transformer who names rivers and provides fish, as well as Coyote and Thunder beings. These accounts preserve ways of understanding the world and the relationships within it. [6, pp. 12–13]

Alsea knowledge holders who helped preserve these traditions included Alsea George, U. S. Grant, William Smith and Thomas Jackson. They worked with Livingston Farrand and Leo J. Frachtenberg. The resulting Alsea Texts and Myths appeared in 1920. Their knowledge and participation made the book possible. [6, pp. 9–11]
Historical change and loss of land

In the early nineteenth century, introduced diseases, including smallpox, severely harmed Alsea communities. At Cape Perpetua, surviving Alsea families nevertheless continued to occupy their homeland into the middle of the century with comparatively limited direct settler influence. [2]

The 1855 Coast Treaty was negotiated but never ratified by the United States Senate. Separately, President Franklin Pierce established the Coast Reservation by executive order on November 9, 1855. It included Alsea homelands and was intended to accommodate many western Oregon peoples. The Alsea therefore experienced the reservation system partly through the incorporation of their own country into a federal reservation. [1, 7]

The Alsea Subagency was a federal administrative unit responsible for several peoples. During the late 1850s and early 1860s, federal officials concentrated Native people in its district, including people removed from Coos and Lower Umpqua homelands. Its history concerns several distinct communities. The name of the agency does not mean everyone held there was Alsea. Conditions included hunger, inadequate shelter and disease. [2, 8]

On December 21, 1865, President Andrew Johnson approved a major reduction of the Coast Reservation around Yaquina Bay. The Siletz Tribe’s account explains that Native villages and farms were still occupied even as officials described the land as unnecessary for Native use. Settlers then forced families from farms in the opened district. [9]

Congress reduced the reservation again on March 3, 1875, eliminating the southern Alsea reservation area. Some people moved north to the remaining Siletz lands while others remained in or returned to coastal communities. The Siletz Tribe records that headmen at Yachats opposed leaving. These measures broke up communities and reduced access to homes, farms and food sources. [8, 10]

Allotment in the early 1890s divided Siletz reservation land into individual parcels. The government then treated much of the remaining land as surplus and acquired it for opening to settlers. The tribal historical account describes this as another major loss of the land base on which families depended. [16]
Language survival and federal restoration

Displacement and disruption of family and village life weakened the passing of Alsea language and stories between generations. Frachtenberg’s introduction itself describes interruptions to winter storytelling. In 1942, Alsea speaker John Albert worked with linguist John Peabody Harrington. Smithsonian archival descriptions identify Albert as the last speaker of Alsea and preserve information about this documentation. The loss of fluent speakers did not end Alsea ancestry or identity. [6, 11]

Federal termination legislation passed in 1954, and termination of the Siletz Tribe was finalized in 1956. Termination ended federal recognition and the associated federal relationship and services. It was a government policy imposed on a continuing people. [12]

After years of organizing, the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians regained federal recognition on November 18, 1977. The Siletz Indian Tribe Restoration Act restored recognition and eligibility for federal services. It did not immediately restore a reservation. Congress established a new, much smaller reservation in 1980. [12, 13]

Alsea descendants continue within the Siletz community. The Tribe supports cultural education, basketry, regalia making and the gathering of traditional materials. Its publicly described language teaching program focuses on Siletz Athabaskan, a different ancestral language from Alsea. These programs belong to a modern confederation whose families carry several distinct cultural histories. [4, 14]

blocks.text: Reading the evidence

Early ethnographers recorded valuable testimony but also edited, translated and judged it through their own assumptions. Frachtenberg explains that he rearranged and sometimes expanded English accounts. One story in the collection was a Coos account translated into Alsea at his request. The book is therefore a mediated record rather than a complete statement of Alsea belief. Tribal accounts help place these records within the history of living communities. [6, pp. 9–12]

blocks.text: Maya History Culture and Timeline
A study of Maya peoples from early farming communities to the present
The Maya and their homelands

The Maya are Indigenous peoples whose homelands include southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and parts of western Honduras and El Salvador. Their history reaches from early farming communities to ancient kingdoms, Spanish colonial rule and the lives of millions of Maya people today. Shared cultural roots connect these peoples, while language, local history and community traditions distinguish them. [1, 3]

Maya society developed across tropical lowlands, volcanic highlands and coastal plains. These environments supported different crops, building materials and trade routes. The ancient Maya formed many kingdoms and alliances rather than a single government ruling the whole Maya world. A capital could dominate neighboring communities without uniting every Maya-speaking people. [3, 5]

Living Maya peoples include the K’iche’, Kaqchikel, Mam, Q’eqchi’, Yucatec Maya, Ch’ol, Tseltal, Tsotsil, Itza and Mopan, among others. Their languages belong to the Mayan language family. These are distinct languages with their own histories. The University of Texas language archive documents this diversity through recordings, stories and other language materials. [2]
Early communities and the first cities

Archaeologists commonly place the Preclassic period around 2000 BCE to 250 CE. Farming villages developed and expanded during this long span. Over time, some communities became large settlements with public plazas, ceremonial buildings and rulers. These dates describe broad changes that occurred at different times in different places. They do not mark a single founding year for the Maya. [25]

Aguada Fénix in present-day Tabasco, Mexico, shows how early people could organize construction on an enormous scale. Excavations and radiocarbon dating place its great platform between about 1000 and 800 BCE. The researchers found little evidence there for the highly unequal royal society familiar from later Maya capitals. They suggest that large communal projects helped shape early public life, although the organization of that work remains a subject of research. [4]

During the later Preclassic, major centers such as El Mirador in northern Guatemala built huge temples and linked settlements with raised roads. Kaminaljuyu became an important highland center. Cities, royal authority and public monuments therefore had deep roots before the Classic period began. [3, 25]
Classic kingdoms and political change

The Classic period, usually dated about 250 to 900 CE, saw extensive city building and the widespread use of dated stone monuments. Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán and other capitals supported royal courts, artists and religious specialists. Buildings included temples, palaces, ball courts and public plazas. Their inscriptions recorded rulers and important events. [5, 22]

Tikal and the Kaan or Snake dynasty associated with Calakmul led competing political networks. Tikal suffered a major defeat in 562 CE. In 695 its ruler Jasaw Chan K’awiil defeated Calakmul, reversing the balance of power. Such conflicts affected allies and smaller kingdoms as well as the largest capitals. [3]

A carved relief from La Pasadita, dated around 770 CE and signed by the sculptor Chakalte’, provides a direct example of political relationships. It shows the local lord Tiloom making an offering to a ruler of Yaxchilán. Its figures and writing present authority as legitimate and honorable. Because a royal patron commissioned such a monument, historians also read it as a political claim rather than an impartial account. [23]

Between roughly the eighth and tenth centuries, many southern lowland kingdoms lost population and political power. Some capitals stopped producing royal inscriptions and maintaining major buildings. Archaeological and climate evidence points to interacting pressures that included warfare, political division, food insecurity and severe drought. Their timing and importance differed by region. A major scholarly review finds that some political problems began before the worst droughts, which makes a single-cause explanation inadequate. [5, 6]

The decline of these kingdoms involved migration and changes in government while Maya communities continued. Northern centers, including Chichén Itzá, became major powers. Later, Mayapán was a leading capital during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Research links its fifteenth-century crisis to drought and factional violence, while also showing that people rebuilt political and economic life outside the city. [7, 22]
Spanish conquest and Maya resistance

Spanish campaigns against Maya kingdoms spread during the sixteenth century. The conquest of the Guatemalan highlands began in 1524, but Spanish control developed unevenly across the wider Maya region. Warfare, introduced diseases, demands for labor and religious persecution disrupted communities. Some Maya leaders fought the invaders, some negotiated and others made alliances shaped by local rivalries. [3, 8, 9]

In 1562, the Franciscan Diego de Landa directed a campaign in Yucatán that included torture and the burning of Maya books and religious objects at Maní. This destruction removed important written records. Colonial testimony must also be handled carefully because statements obtained through torture or threats cannot simply be accepted as reliable descriptions of Maya belief or practice. [8]

The Itza kingdom in northern Guatemala remained independent long after the first Spanish invasions. On March 13, 1697, Spanish troops captured its island capital, Nojpeten, in Lake Petén Itzá. The fall of this last major independent Maya kingdom did not end local resistance. Forced relocation, disease and further rebellion followed. [9]

Colonial rule and later independence from Spain left many Maya communities facing heavy taxes, land loss and unequal treatment. In 1847, a major rebellion began in Yucatán, commonly called the Caste War. Its causes included disputes over communal land, burdens on villagers and struggles within regional politics. Maya-speaking rebels established independent communities in the southeast. Their political autonomy endured until a major Mexican military offensive in 1901, though that date did not resolve every local conflict. [10, 11]
The twentieth century and living Maya peoples

Guatemala’s civil war lasted from 1960 to 1996. Maya civilians suffered massacres, displacement and the destruction of communities. The Historical Clarification Commission reported in 1999 that Maya people made up 83 percent of the victims it identified. It found that army attacks against Maya groups between 1981 and 1983 included acts of genocide. These findings describe documented state violence; they do not mean that all Maya people shared one political position during the war. [12, 13]

Rigoberta Menchú Tum, a K’iche’ Maya advocate, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992 for her work for social justice and Indigenous rights. Her public work helped draw international attention to the treatment of Indigenous peoples in Guatemala. Peace agreements ended the civil war in 1996, while demands for truth and justice continued. [13, 14]

Maya history also includes continuing efforts to protect land. In Belize, an April 2015 consent order of the Caribbean Court of Justice recognized that Maya customary land tenure in Toledo District creates constitutionally protected property rights. The court’s later judgment addressed the state’s obligations and remedies. This was a specific victory for the affected communities, not a declaration settling all Maya land claims across the region. [15]

Today, Maya people live in rural communities, cities and migrant communities abroad. They work in many occupations and take part in contemporary political and cultural life. Maya organizations promote language, ancestral knowledge and Indigenous rights. The International Maya League describes its work as connecting present needs with inherited knowledge while respecting differences among Maya peoples. [1, 24]
Culture and everyday life

Food and land use. Maize, beans, squash and chiles are central to many Maya food traditions. The milpa is a system of cultivation that can include mixed crops and a long cycle of managed regrowth. In forest-garden systems, farmers encourage useful plants as fields return to woodland. This requires knowledge of soils, plants and seasonal conditions. Maya agriculture has varied across regions and periods rather than following one fixed method. [16]

Language and community. Language carries family history, oral literature and local knowledge. K’iche’ and Kaqchikel are related, as are Tseltal and Tsotsil, but related languages remain distinct. Language use and the strength of transmission to children vary by community. The materials held by language archives also show Maya people speaking, singing and telling stories in their own languages. [2]

Writing and books. Ancient Maya writing represented spoken language through signs for words and syllables. Scribes wrote on monuments and portable objects as well as in folding books called codices. Decipherment allows historians to identify individuals and events that earlier researchers could not read. The surviving royal texts emphasize the concerns of rulers and their courts, so archaeology remains essential for understanding ordinary households. [17, 23]

Mathematics and calendars. Maya mathematics included a developed use of zero. Their calendars included a 260-day sacred cycle, a 365-day Haab cycle and a Long Count that located events across much longer spans. Calendar names and practices differ by language and region. Some communities continue to consult trained daykeepers. Calendar knowledge connected observations of the sky with ritual and agricultural life. [17, 18]

Religion and sacred authority. Ancient Maya religion recognized many divine beings associated with rain, maize, celestial cycles and other aspects of existence. Kings and queens performed rituals that supported their claims to rule. Some ceremonies included royal bloodletting or human sacrifice, but the form and intensity varied. These practices must be understood through their particular historical settings. [8, 19]

The Popol Vuh. This work preserves a K’iche’ account of creation, origins and spiritual history. The surviving Newberry manuscript was copied by Francisco Ximénez around 1700 to 1715, with K’iche’ text beside a Spanish translation. It preserves older traditions through a colonial manuscript. Its date, language and transmission matter: it should not be treated as an unchanged book shared by every Maya people. [20]

Art and architecture. Maya artists worked in stone, stucco, wood, clay, shell and jade. They created royal portraits, painted vessels and images of divine beings. Some artists signed their work. The traces of pigment preserved on the La Pasadita relief show that sculpture could be brightly colored. Temples and palaces formed part of a built environment that also included ordinary homes and spaces for public activity. [5, 22, 23]

Weaving and clothing. Maya textile traditions continue through skilled work and changing designs. A huipil is a woven or embroidered garment whose form differs across communities. Its colors, patterns and construction can indicate a person’s community, though styles are flexible and change over time. The University of Oklahoma’s collections show marked differences even within a single language group. [21]
How historians study Maya history

Maya history draws on excavated buildings, household remains, environmental evidence, inscriptions, manuscripts and living testimony. Each source answers different questions. Royal carvings promote rulers, colonial accounts often reflect missionary aims and modern communities bring knowledge that older scholarship overlooked. Comparing these forms of evidence helps explain both political change and the continued lives of Maya peoples. [6, 8, 20, 23, 24]
